Developing applications that require strong consistency across distributed systems can be challenging.  A design approach for Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) is lacking, which hinders the creation of efficient and consistent data structures across multiple systems.  A design pattern for Multi-valued Update CRDTs has been common practice, but this approach is not universally applicable and does not account for systems that follow different convergence criteria.  This paper presents a first-ever design framework for various types of CRDTs, including Multi-valued Update CRDTs, Single-valued Update CRDTs, and Delete CRDTs.  By identifying fundamental characteristics of each CRDT type and a general process for creating new designs, this framework enables the development of new and adapted data structures for different convergence strategies.  As proof of concept, this study creates three novel data structures: a Multi-valued Update CRDT called $Set^{+}$, which can handle duplicate elements; a Multi-valued Insert/Update CRDT called $Bag$, which uses unique elements; and a Delete CRDT called $List_{\bot}$, which can handle element removal.  An analysis of the designed data structures' consistency, accuracy, and performance is provided, showcasing that they outperform existing practice implementations.  Furthermore, this study demonstrates the application of $Set^{+}$ and $List_{\bot}$ in actual use cases, highlighting the practical applications and advantages of using well-designed CRDTs.  By offering a design framework and novel data structures, this study addresses existing limitations and provides useful design patterns for creating new and effective Consistent Data Structures for Distributed Systems.  All implemented data structures, as well as the associated design documents, are available for public use and can be downloaded from our supplementary website.  We recommend using these designs as a foundation for the development of additional CRDT types, with the aim of creating a comprehensive library of consistent data structures for distributed systems.  We hope this study will contribute to the advancement of Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, enabling the creation of powerful and efficient distributed applications. To explore the impact of proteins on genotypic influences, we developed a method
to map phenotype-associated SNPs to proteins. Using a comprehensive approach
combining 15 types of evidence, we identified a significant correlation between
protein sequences and the geographic distribution of SNPs associated with certain
traits. The effect of protein sequence on the distribution of associated SNPs
varies greatly among different traits, as does the geographic extent of SNPs.
In many cases, the primary protein target explains a substantial portion of the
variation in the geographic distribution of associated SNPs. Our approach can
also pinpoint specific amino acid residues within a protein that contribute to
the variation in the geographic distribution of associated SNPs. By applying our
method to a range of traits, from blood biochemistry to susceptibility to
infectious diseases, we found that protein sequence influences the distribution of
associated SNPs to a considerable degree, with an average effect size of 0.41.
Our study demonstrates the utility of our approach in exploring the link
between protein function and the geographic distribution of associated SNPs, and
it paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of the genetic basis
of geographic variation in human populations. Our approach and results are now
available on our user-friendly website at https://geosnps.org.

To determine if the semantic diversity of responses can be increased through the use of other dialogues, we propose examining the relationship between dialogues with different semantic meanings. However, establishing a clear cut-off point to measure the degree of semantic diversity is not straightforward. In this paper, we first present an alternative method to analyze the semantic diversity of dialogues. Based on this analysis, we investigate the role of other dialogues with the same intent but different semantic meanings in answer generation. Next, we examine the impact of dialogues with different semantic meanings on the same intent. Finally, we discuss design options for a neutral generator that can produce diverse semantic responses. To this end, we propose a simple approach utilizing minimum and maximum semantics based on response distributions. A more advanced approach involving attention mechanisms on dialogue state is also explored. Evaluations indicate that both attention-based and fully connected models are capable of generating diverse semantic responses, with attention-based models performing better according to both automatic and human assessment metrics. Notably, the results show that simply adding additional data with the same intent but different semantic meanings can significantly improve both intent classification and dialogue generation performance. Moreover, even without a separate evaluation set, our proposed approach allows for controlling the degree of semantic diversity in response generation. In some cases, our method achieves similar performance to baseline models that do not consider semantic diversity, and outperforms models that do not take intent into account. However, there is still room for improvement in this study, and possible avenues for further research are discussed. All code and data used in this research are available online for replication and further exploration. In addition, pre-generated models and evaluation tools are provided for easy access to both the datasets and models employed in this paper.

In graph theory, splitting vertices is a well-known technique used to convert non-planar graphs into planar counterparts. We investigate the effect of removing vertices by splitting on planarity in bipartite graphs. Specifically, we examine a method where each vertex is replaced by an edge that connects two new vertices, and we aim to minimize the number of these new vertices needed to planarize the graph. We prove that for any bipartite graph, using this method results in a subgraph with a number of new vertices no more than twice the number of original vertices. Furthermore, we establish that this approach is almost optimal, as there are instances where the number of new vertices required approaches the number of original vertices. We also present a more efficient strategy that splits fewer vertices, though it only applies to a limited class of transitive bipartite graphs. In general, however, we demonstrate that a significant improvement in the number of new vertices cannot be achieved, addressing a related open question posed by Fialowski and Pitz. Additionally, we identify a fundamental limitation of splitting vertex algorithms in graph theory. Lastly, we contribute to the study of vertex-splitting operations in planarity testing and graph drawing by introducing new concepts and resolving several open questions. We showcase an algorithm capable of detecting when a graph can be planarized through vertex splitting, and this algorithm serves as the basis for a vertex-splitting feature in a graph drawing tool. We also examine various properties of recursively applied vertex-splitting operations and investigate relationships between these operations and other planarity testing methods. Lastly, we discuss potential directions for further research in this area.

Closed-loop feedback control is a key factor in bipedal robots' dynamic performance, particularly during gait cycles, when its intricate walking pattern may lead to divergent movements. To test the compensatory effects of closed-loop feedback in bipedal robots, a simple and generalizable method is proposed using forced response analysis. This method is applied to a nonlinear, physically-based bipedal robot model, featuring a straight upper body and non-collocated heel-toe foot movement. The analysis involves introducing an external force onto the foot, which excites the closed-loop system and forces it to walk while being subjected to a recurring force. The resulting movement in both time and frequency domains is then used to evaluate how closed-loop feedback affects the robot's ability to withstand this external force. It is shown that by carefully designing the closed-loop feedback, the robot is able to reduce the amplitude of this excitation-induced movement. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the frequency response of the bipedal robot is distinct from that of its linearized counterpart due to its nonlinear movement. Lastly, it is found that the direction of this frequency response depends on the direction of gait cycle movement. To validate the analytical findings, discrete-time nonlinear simulations are conducted using MATLAB/Simulink, along with a robust control system to filter out oscillations. The match between analytical and simulated frequency responses is found to be excellent. To further explore the impact of closed-loop feedback, an experiment using a nonlinear, physically-based bipedal robot is designed, involving the excitation of the closed-loop system during gait cycles with an external force. The results of this experiment are found to align with the analytical and simulation findings. Ultimately, this study provides a method for evaluating closed-loop feedback in bipedal robots through forced response analysis, which can be used to design more effective feedback controllers. Additionally, this study highlights the significance of considering the nonlinear dynamics of bipedal robots in such analyses. 

Keywords: Bipedal robots, closed-loop feedback, forced response analysis, nonlinear dynamics, non-collocated actuation, robust control systems, experimental validation.

Recent Flush+Reload attacks have achieved significant success in detecting side-channel leaks on various platforms. However, these attacks are limited by the time resolution of the system cache and memory access map, which can only distinguish cache flush and memory access after an average of one second or up to a few tens of milliseconds. Additionally, existing Flush+Reload attacks require multiple memory access traces to an array of different sizes, making them time-consuming and impractical for modern applications with large data structures. To address these limitations, we propose HyperDegrade, a new technique that dramatically enhances the time resolution and reduces the number of required traces. By combining multiple Flush+Reload attacks with different access patterns, HyperDegrade can accurately detect secret data access sizes exceeding 64 bytes and can distinguish between access sizes larger than 20 bytes. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade on detecting a range of platforms, including modern x86-64 and PowerPC servers. Moreover, we show that HyperDegrade can detect various memory access patterns, such as array accesses and stack frame allocations, without any prior knowledge of the application's source code or binary. Our findings confirm that HyperDegrade can effectively leverage the complexity of application memory access patterns to increase its detection accuracy. We also explore other attack scenarios, including detecting data caches and indirect calls, and provide guidelines for optimizing HyperDegrade's performance in different scenarios. A comprehensive evaluation of HyperDegrade's performance is conducted on various applications and platforms. Finally, we outline potential future directions for improving HyperDegrade's efficacy and versatility. This pull-back doesn't yield a well-defined rational function, but rather a valuation on the source, which we can use to extend the original morphism to a harmonic morphism between valuations on the source and target. Here, we show that when the morphism is finite and bijective, for any valuation on the source, the pull-back of the rational function, determined by the morphism and the valuation, forms a rational function. Furthermore, this establishes a Galois connection with pulling back rational functions on the source, and we explore additional properties of this relationship. These results can be viewed as an instance of a broader, more general construction where we consider harmonic morphisms between tropical curves as "functions" to pull back rational functions. Finally, we apply these findings to a related problem involving the Galois relations between fields of functions on tropical curves. These fields are obtained through pull-backs of the rational function semifield under harmonic morphisms between curves, and they exhibit a hierarchical structure reflecting the graph of the harmonic morphism. The stability of white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes was re-examined taking into account the impact of neutrino oscillations on their mass determination. It was found that a significant effect on this relationship occurs when the sum of the three neutrino mass states reaches approximately 0.3-0.4 eV, which also coincides with the lower limit for the smallest neutrino mass state. If this condition is met, the stability of these cosmic objects would only be guaranteed when their total neutrino mass is at least 0.3-0.4 eV. Otherwise, their stability relies on the minimum of the neutrino mass spectrum, with a maximum allowance of 0.07 eV. Consequently, the accuracy required for future neutron star radius measurements should be no worse than 5-10 km to effectively test the neutrino mass hypothesis through this relationship. Furthermore, in scenarios where the neutrino mass spectrum is quasi-degenerate, even a stable neutron star could transform into a black hole if the neutrinos are released during the star's formation process. This research highlights the interconnectedness of neutrino physics and the properties of compact objects, which could provide valuable insights into neutrino properties through future multi-messenger observations of compact object events. Lastly, it was found that neutron star mergers could offer a more suitable laboratory to study neutrino physics, given their immense energy equivalent to roughly 10% of the solar energy output and lasting several seconds, allowing for an examination of neutrino processes that could influence the post-merger dynamics. Nonetheless, the current understanding of these events precludes a more detailed investigation of this aspect. Nonetheless, this research lays the groundwork for further exploration of the interplay between neutrinos and compact objects, given their significant implications for our comprehension of these cosmic entities and the fundamental neutrino properties. Ultimately, this study suggests that a deeper examination of this relationship will not only provide novel neutrino-related phenomena to investigate but also yield new avenues for studying neutrino physics in contexts beyond particle physics experiments. Consequently, this research proposes a fresh paradigm in the interconnection of astrophysics and particle physics, where the study of compact objects and neutrinos can now be seen as an integrated endeavor that benefits from this new perspective. The C++ library, seal, is an open-source collection of high-performance matrix functions that leverages parallel computing through the tbb and omp threading libraries for improved efficiency. seal has been successfully applied to solve various real-world problems in fields like signal processing, machine learning, and linear algebra. The library's matrix functions are now accessible via R through the RSeAL package, enabling users to take advantage of parallel computing from within R. This talk will introduce the features and technical details of seal, present its applications and showcase its performance improvements, and also cover the new RSeAL package for easy R seal library integration. Specifically, we will highlight the challenges and advantages of programming with parallel algorithms and threaded bindings, as well as the benefits and results of using seal with RSeAL in machine learning contexts. Additionally, we will present recent research using seal to speed up iterative solvers and deep neural network training on GPU. The talk will also include an evaluation of seal's performance when solving large linear systems and training large datasets with stochastic gradient descent. The goals of this talk are to promote the use of high-performance numerical computations in R and to encourage collaboration to achieve greater performance and usability in R's matrix computations. The seal library is now available on CRAN and can be downloaded via install.packages("RSeAL"). This study conducts an in-depth examination of privacy vulnerabilities in the context of vertical federated learning (VFL). We first outline the theoretical foundations of differential privacy in learning and then examine the practical applications of VFL in various contexts. We then outline the limitations of previous research in this area and identify the need for more comprehensive study in this field. Building on existing work, we particularly focus on privacy breaches occurring when the user's data is shared with untrusted third parties or organizations. We then outline a framework for categorizing and analyzing privacy breaches in VFL, and discuss the feasibility of particular attacks against multi-key VFL protocols. We also demonstrate the practical applicability of these attacks by carrying out an actual-world test between a training institution and a company that are VFL participants. The results show that the company can recover users' sensitive information with high accuracy, indicating that VFL may pose a risk of privacy breaches in real-world applications. We also propose a simple and effective solution to mitigate these breaches. In recent years, Random Fourier Features have been widely used as a cost-effective method for expanding kernel methods to high-dimensional spaces. However, RFF is limited by its low accuracy due to its random generation of features. To address this issue, we propose Pseudo-Random Fourier Features, which uses an optimized strategy to reduce features dimensionality while improving prediction performance. Compared to traditional RFF, PRFF has lower generalization errors, outperforming RFF in classification and regression tasks. Moreover, PRFF maintains complementary stability and is adaptable to various kernel methods, including support vector machines and neural networks. We examine the theoretical aspects of PRFF and evaluate its practical applications through experiments on real-world datasets. Our results demonstrate that PRFF yields superior performance over RFF in multiple scenarios. Additionally, PRFF facilitates interpretation by generating a pseudo input that is correlated with the prediction outcome, which can be used to improve models by identifying anomalies. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulame/PRFF.

A leading challenge in the field of cardiac machine learning is the automated segmentation of images from various modalities, including MRI and echocardiography. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of deep learning models in this area; however, there is still a significant gap in understanding how these models generalize across different modalities and patient populations with varying levels of cardiac pathology. To investigate this, we established a public database consisting of four datasets, included data from two modalities (MRI and 2D and 3D echocardiography) with associated annotations, and organized it into the Cardiac Segmentation Generalizability (CSG) database. We selected four strong baseline models with proven performance in cardiac segmentation and conducted thorough generalization and robustness tests across the CSG database. The evaluation revealed that even the best-performing networks showed a significant decline in accuracy when applied to datasets with pathology levels different from those present in the training dataset. Notably, networks overestimated their performance when compared to their actual generalization capacity. To address this issue, we proposed a novel metric called the Generalization Error Distribution (GED) to assess the degree of true vs. predicted performance divergence. Through GED analysis, we identified that networks tend to generalize better to datasets with similar levels of pathology and that pediATRIA, a dataset with complex anatomy, poses a significant challenge for generalization. Ultimately, our study provided valuable insights into the generalizability of cardiac segmentation models and introduced the GED metric to facilitate more effective evaluation of models in this domain. However, we found that even the best-performing networks struggled to generalize across different modalities, highlighting the need for more research in this area. Current models excel at following complex instructions in the language domain, but they struggle with unstructured instructions that incorporate a variety of inputs, including visual information and text, for tasks like organizing files and planning events. In response, we've developed a new task and dataset, called MultiModal TACO, which assesses a machine's ability to understand and act upon instructions composed of several components, without regard to order, using tools like file folders and a calendar. The impact of a small-scale disturbance in a complex network can be dramatically amplified through a process known as avalanche cascades. Investigating this phenomenon is crucial especially for understanding the spread of ideas, rumors, and diseases as well as the economic and financial crises. This work introduces two advanced statistical measures to analyze avalanche activity - size distribution and a newly devised degree distribution resulting from an avalanche, which are applied to examine the fragmentation of a scientific collaboration network following a removal of a single node. Our analysis indicates that both the pre- and post-fragments of the network exhibit power-law characteristics. Notably, the indication that averages are not sufficient in this case is provided by the ratio of the two relevant exponents falling short of 1, displaying distinct values before and after the network's disruption. Moreover, our results suggest that the origin and destination of a node may influence its ability to withstand subsequent removals triggered by an initial event, an aspect yet to be explored in existing studies. All data and corresponding analysis are freely accessible at https://doi.org/10.6082/ M1DW4XWB.

One specific variant, the generalized sextic Freud weight, can be obtained from a more general formula for weights of the Freud type by setting $p=6$ and $q=2$. This form stands in marked contrast to the generalized Airy weight, which takes the form $x^l e^{-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{n}\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right)^l$ for some non-negative integer $l$. It has been established that orthogonal polynomials in relation to the generalized sextic Freud weight or the generalized Airy weight exhibit limits of some $n$ in the limit $p\to 2$ (or equivalently, $q\to 1$) or $l\to 0$ respectively, with these limits equating to the original Freud or Airy forms. Furthermore, it has been found that by adjusting the index in a specific manner, the standard damped harmonic oscillator equation can be transformed into an equivalent form expressible as a product of two differential equations, one being a Schr\"{o}dinger equation with a potential corresponding to the generalized sextic Freud weight, with the other being a singular Sine-Gordon equation. This potential exhibits the mentioned limit $p\to 2$ (or $q\to 1$) or $l\to 0$ for all cases of interest, thereby demonstrating a direct relationship between the generalized sextic Freud weight and the damped harmonic oscillator equation. Additionally, it is shown that a similar relationship exists between the generalized Airy weight and the stationary superradialized Toda molecule equation. Lastly, this paper introduces an operator that converts a given weight to an associated "supersymmetric partner", and it is demonstrated that this transformation is equivalent to either changing the index in the above mentioned manner, or altering the potential in the Schr\"{o}dinger equation. A novel design for a gravitational wave detector, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, is introduced. This new configuration incorporates a complex optical layout that uses a central suspended test mass to modify the Sagnac interferometer's signal recycling system. The design offers enhanced sensitivity at specific low-frequency ranges compared to standard interferometer designs, particularly in scenarios where thermal noise from the mirror surfaces becomes a significant limiting factor. A mathematical model has been developed to analyze the behavior of the sloshing-Sagnac design and its equivalent simple suspended test mass system in the context of advanced gravitational wave detectors. The study demonstrates that the sloshing-Sagnac design yields improved sensitivity in the 10-100 Hz frequency range; however, above 100 Hz both design formats exhibit comparable sensitivity. The research also reveals that the proposed design format can match the ultimate noise floor when taking into account mirror material imperfections and other sources of thermal noise. In this paper, we examine the performance of random access in extremely large-scale MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems and propose a new non-orthogonal variable spacing pilot reuse protocol called NOVR-XL for reducing co-channel interference. We analyze the output signal-to-interference ratio of NOVR-XL and derive an estimate for the maximum achievable throughput per unit area in a two-dimensional cellular network. Compared to existing MIMO RAC schemes, NOVR-XL significantly enhances RAC performance by a factor of $\sqrt{N_t}$, where $N_t$ represents the number of antenna per base station, and is therefore particularly suitable for XL-MIMO systems. Numerical simulations validate our analytical findings and reveal NOVR-XL's ability to adapt to varying XL-MIMO configurations. Furthermore, NOVR-XL is shown to outperform state-of-the-art MIMO RAC schemes, such as OR-WFMA and PFR, by as much as $10^5$ times in terms of throughput per unit area. Additionally, NOVR-XL's performance benefits are expected to carry over to other XL-MIMO applications.

The formation of planetary systems is attributed to the evolution of protoplanetary disks.
Over time, the dissipation of these disks allows for the formation of solid structures,
which can develop into planetesimals, paving the way for the creation of planets.
Research indicates that small, isolated solid grains are incapable of own thermodynamic stability,
thus requiring a reevaluation of their formation processes.
A study using the DUSTYY code, a thermal evolution model for protoplanetary disks,
found that substructures in disks can foster the formation of planetesimals through heating
of solid particles within designated hot zones.
Additionally, studies employing the Herschel and ALMA have revealed that protoplanetary disks
possess multiple solid substructures, including ridges, cavities, and rings.
These substructures could serve as "staircases" for the cumulative growth of solid grains,
enabling the formation of planetesimals in the outer disk regions. 
A new framework for planetary formation has been proposed, incorporating the grain growth
process into the disk's evolutionary cycle, and could provide a viable pathway for the exoplanet population to form. 
Further empirical evidence from current and upcoming observational surveys will be necessary
to validate this theoretical model. 
In turn, this could shed light on the fundamental processes that shape planetary systems. 
A potential pathway to the population of small to medium-sized planets has been proposed,
involving the gradual accumulation of solid grains across multiple substructures,
while large planets may emerge from a single giant substructure,
enabling a more refined approach to modeling planetary formation. 
A future direction for research involves incorporating the proposed model into a full
planetary formation simulation, utilizing a parallel code structure, to explore its implications
for planetary system architecture. 
Ultimately, this could provide a new perspective on the formation of planetary systems,
one that is intimately connected to the evolution of protoplanetary disks. 
In this research, multiple formation pathways for planetesimals and planets are being
identified, offering a more nuanced understanding of how planetary systems come to be. 
This study also highlights the significance of substructures in protoplanetary disks,
emphasizing their role as "staircases" for grain growth and planatesimal formation,
and positions itself for contributions to ongoing and future observational surveys,
as well as a deeper exploration of the population of small to medium-sized planets. 
Ultimately, this research aims to evolve the field of planetary formation beyond traditional modeling.

This research focuses on creating frequency-resistant Molmer-Sorensen gates for ion chains and examines how these gates impact entanglement development. A theoretical model is presented, along with an implementation strategy using a mixed entanglement metric. Through numerical analysis, the effects of variation in drive frequency, amplitude, and duration on gate robustness and entanglement are investigated. It is demonstrated that specific design choices can minimize the impact of frequency errors and increase entanglement levels, even in large chains. An experimental approach is also described to test the efficacy of these gates. Finally, this study indicates that Molser gates can serve as a reliable means of entanglement accumulation in ion chains, particularly in scenarios where frequent calibration is not feasible. This work has significant implications for the implementation of quantum error correction codes in ion traps.

We take a deep dive into mutational dynamics of Laurent polynomials through their combinatorial representation via tropical graphs, specifically focusing on the dynamics of their mutation classes. By exploring the properties of these classes, we establish a connection to Fano 3-folds, particularly proving that classes of certain Laurent polynomials, related to 3-fold Fano varieties with specific properties, can be completely determined. This involves showing that such classes are in one-to-one correspondence with the parameters of these varieties, and that this relationship is highly structured. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mutational dynamics of these Laurent polynomials result in a comprehensive set of distinct mutation classes, which are directly linked to the families of Fano 3-folds that exhibit various levels of extremality properties. A single face image can capture an entire range of 3D face information. However, when analyzing face images, changes in lighting and expression can confuse conventional face analysis techniques. To tackle this issue, we propose a method called Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) that uses two separate learned representations for pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. It works by first using a factor learned from a pose-independent representation to align the input image with a reference face, and then uses the aligned image and the remaining pose-dependent representation to reconstruct the input face. This allows us to separate pose-dependent and pose-independent factors that were previously conflated, ultimately enabling us to manipulate factor changes that were previously mixed up. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that SADRNet can successfully decompose face images into pose-dependent and pose-independent factors, and that its factor learning is more robust and less prone to overfitting. It outperforms current state-of-the-art methods that use similar approaches, and is particularly effective at processing images of unknown poses, and can be used for both face reconstruction and analysis tasks. It also provides a more intuitive way of interpreting face analysis results, and can be used for multiple applications such as face editing, and analysis tasks like expression and accessory detection. It also shows potential for low-light face analysis, and can be used to improve other face analysis techniques. All source code and models are available online.

This approach is significant because traditional low-rank approximations often fail to capture the benefits of over-parameterized models, especially in scenarios with evolving variables. By employing an approximate posterior distribution through a multivariate probit function with Gaussian alternatives, we are able to conduct inference and generate compact expressions for the expected log-likelihood and its derivatives, enabling the application of efficient optimization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on synthetic and real-world datasets, including a an experiment with the Boston housing dataset, and show that it outperforms alternative low-rank approximation methods. Current active learning methodologies suffer from significant variability in their performance when applied to large-scale datasets like ImageNet, in contrast to their reliable results on smaller benchmark datasets. This study suggests that the success of these methods on smaller datasets is attributed to the overlap between the initial and expanded datasets. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of a diverse proxy set, which is used to evaluate the effectiveness of each sampling algorithm. The results of our experiments indicate that traditional active learning algorithms are prone to noise and diverse proxy sets are crucial for their reliability. Furthermore, our findings show that DeepCoAL, a recent advanced algorithm, may not be the optimal choice for large-scale datasets due to its high computational costs. We also propose an alternative approach, Sample-wise Coarse Aggregation (SWCA), that leverages the overlap between datasets to achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced computational costs. The experimental results demonstrate that SWCA achieves comparable performance to DeepCoAL while incurring only a tenth of the computational overhead. We have open-sourced our code and dataset annotations for the considered benchmarks at https://github.com/whonyy/SWCA.

We investigate the application of two-mode squeezing in quantum-enhanced phase sensing, using a resource state generated via linear optical devices. A constraint is identified that maximizes the Fisher information, leading to improved performance, and we demonstrate the feasibility of this approach using paraxial quantum optics. Two-mode squeezing is shown to provide an explicit advantage over single-mode squeezing in phase-sensing applications. Additionally, we examine the relationship between this technique and quantum metrology scenarios involving multiple input modes, and propose a related strategy using three modes of light for improved phase-sensing sensitivity. This approach, involving two-mode squeezing and feedback, is shown to surpass the classical phase-sensing limit in the interferometer phase-sensing scenario. Two distinct strategies are compared for generating two-mode squeezing, including one that yields a success probability for the quantum non-demolition parity gate that is twice as high as another method. We also find that in certain cases, using single-mode squeezing can actually decrease the required two-mode squeezing, resulting in greater phase-sensing sensitivity. Finally, we examine the application of this technique to the measurement of an optical phase in an interferometer, and demonstrate its practical viability.

We analyze the spin functionality of a silicon double-donor device with a staggered configuration, utilizing two distinct sets of donor placements and tuning their Rydberg-like states through applied voltages. We examine both unbiased and applied voltage scenarios to determine the impact on two-qubit logic gates and single-qubit operations. In the first case, without bias, the spin states remain entangled and the performance of the two-qubit gate is nearly fault-tolerant, while in the second case, with appropriate bias, the spin states can be adjusted to optimize the two-qubit gate's fidelity, enabling the execution of multiple operations without the need for donor re-tuning. We also investigate the influence of ion spin states, charge states, and noise on the performance of the two-qubit gate and find that a systematically controlled approach can mitigate these factors' impact. Furthermore, we investigate the sensitivity of the double donor system to its environment and find that certain states exhibit decreased interaction with the surrounding lattice, providing the potential for robust operation in the presence of lattice defects. A comparison with a silicon-surface code reveals that a double donor device can offer a significant increase in storage capacity, with a cavity-controlled setup enabling even greater efficiency gains. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that a double donor device offers a promising platform for the realization of quantum computing at the silicon level.

This research paper proposes an innovative adaptive cooperative nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) protocol that dynamically switches between cooperative and noncooperative modes based on the quality of the direct link. The proposed protocol is then analyzed to determine its outage probability, which serves as a benchmark for comparing its performance to other advanced protocols, including D2D communication systems that utilize NOMA and LCME. The proposed protocol's outcome probability is mathematically derived to demonstrate its superior performance in terms of outage probability, with the protocol's adaptive nature providing a significant improvement in this metric, especially in scenarios with high values of $\gamma_d$ or $P_s/P_d$. The proposed protocol's results are then validated through Monte Carlo simulations, which also enable the investigation of how the protocol's performance is affected by different relaying strategies, including AF and DF, as well as the impact of increasing $K$ on the outcome probability. The proposed protocol is found to offer superior performance in all investigated scenarios. The adaptive cooperative NOMA protocol is also found to provide a significant improvement in outage probability when compared to other advanced protocols, including NOMA-D2D and LCME, especially in scenarios with high values of $\gamma_d$ or $P_s/P_d$. The proposed protocol's results also reveal that the DF relaying strategy yields better outcome probability performance than the AF strategy, although the difference in performance is relatively minor. Lastly, the investigation finds that the outcome probability performance remains relatively insensitive to the number of users $K$, especially in the high signal power regime. The proposed protocol's results also provide valuable insights into the design of future NOMA-based D2D communication systems, including the optimal selection of the activation threshold $\gamma_t$. The proposed protocol's results may be used to guide the development of efficient activation and decoding schemes, especially in scenarios with multiple D2D users. We examine the structure of a specific 4-tensor that has been linked to studies of matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological order, with the goal of identifying its factorized forms and the associated symmetry of the corresponding interacting lattice models. We establish a connection between the 4-tensor and the fusion algebra associated with a particular quantum double, specifically for the case of abelian anyons in (1+1) dimensions. We then generalize our analysis to the context of non-abelian anyons and find that the 4-tensor can be utilized to create a resource state that allows for exact expressions of matrix product operators related to the non-abelian fusion algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these models exhibit both chiral and gapless properties, with the central charge being equivalent to the number of semi-simple Lie algebras generated by the anyons. Additionally, we explore and calculate specific matrix product operators for both abelian and non-abelian anyons, with the case of Ising anyons also being explicitly considered. Lastly, we propose that interacting lattice models based on non-abelian anyons could be used to mimic the physics of Wessel-Zamolodchikov c-theorem in 1+1 dimensions. All necessary algebraic details for the non-abelian anyons are explicitly outlined in the paper.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable performance on complex NLP tasks, yet they can still struggle with minor changes to input text. Data augmentation methods have emerged as a key tool for mitigating this issue, by transforming and diversifying the training data. While many augmentation techniques exist, little research has focused on understanding how these methods impact both training and testing. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an in-depth analysis of five popular augmentation techniques, involving pseudo-labeling, word dropout, masking, replacement, and concatenation. Our findings revealed that different methods have distinct effects on both model training and performance, with some augmentations exerting a significant influence on both. To generalize these findings across multiple models, we also explored the interaction between augmentation and three different types of neural network components: input representations, loss functions, and optimization algorithms. Our results showed that pseudo-labeling and concatenation primarily impact model training, but also have a notable effect on test performance. In contrast, word dropout and replacement primarily affect test performance. Our research also identified that some augmentation techniques can be used to achieve better performance without any augmentation during test time. To facilitate future research, we have made our extensive dataset and experimentation framework publicly available, providing a foundation for exploring additional augmentation methods and testing hypotheses. By continuing to build upon these findings, we can continue to advance the field of data augmentation in NLP. Additionally, we introduce a new classification of augmentation techniques as primary or secondary, with respect to their influence on model training, and offer our findings as a starting point for further exploration. Our work is a critical initial step towards creating a comprehensive theory of data augmentation in NLP, and we invite the community to contribute to and build upon our research. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/ghulad/data-augmentation-analysis.git

When machine learning models rely on graph-structured input data, extending the usual differential privacy framework proves complicated due to interconnected input points. In our work, we investigate the challenges of privacy loss computation in connection to data points that are connected to each other, specifically in the context of private spectral graph learning. Our contribution involves analyzing differentially private private spectral graph learning with a specific focus on the Laplace noise mechanism and examining various combinations of graph properties and learning parameters that affect privacy loss computation. Our findings reveal that privacy loss can be complicated to calculate due to interconnected input points, yet we investigate methods for approximating it. Our proposed approximation techniques can be utilized for optimizing noise levels in private learning, which is demonstrated through our experiments and extensions to private community detection are also provided. Our results show that these approximation techniques are effective, especially in scenarios where precise computation is challenging. Our implementation is available online at: https://github.com/anonymous-author/priv-sgl. Our work has potential to contribute to the development of private learning algorithms that are adaptable to diverse real-world graph datasets.

As a result, this method can efficiently identify and pinpoint weaknesses in automated lane-keeping systems, streamlining the development process. Ultimately, this approach is anticipated to contribute to the creation of reliable and robust automated lane-keeping systems for vehicles. The personalization of music playlists has become a common practice, where recommendations are made based on the audio content within the playlist. Traditional methods rely on user feedback and audio features extracted through content analysis. This report explores the benefits of music playlists as self-expression tools, highlighting the unique insights users convey through their listening habits. Building on existing research, our content analysis techniques leverage machine learning models to extract audio features from music tracks and gauge user preferences from listening data. By correlating audio content with user preferences, we identified several key factors that influence these preferences. To streamline the recommendation process, we tested various techniques, including classification models and similarity metrics. Results from these experiments informed the development of a simplified recommendation approach, combining collaborative filtering with weighted scoring. This method yields promising outcomes and lays the groundwork for further refinement. Notably, our findings indicate that music playlists, despite being a form of self-expression, still align with underlying listener preferences. Nevertheless, our research uncovered distinct differences in song popularity across various listening contexts. Moreover, we observed instances where a song's presence in a playlist contradicts the overall user preference, suggesting that music playlists sometimes prioritize expression over personal taste. By exploring these insights, we hope to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the role of music playlists in artist discovery and promotion. Additionally, our studies on audio content analysis and user preference prediction provide a foundation for more sophisticated recommendation approaches, which can learn from listening data and produce tailored music playlists that align with individual tastes. As a result, we propose a framework for automated music playlist recommendation, which we believe has the potential to shape the future of the music industry. This report serves as an overview of our research, and we invite readers to delve into the accompanying thesis for more in-depth information.

A linearized hydrodynamic method for electrons has been adapted into a stochastic version to simulate the dynamics of electronic non-equilibrium quantum correlations. This new algorithm was applied to study the dynamics of capillary waves in a quantum drift-diffusion model, inspired by the scenario of an electron source in a semiconductor device. The simulation reveals an exponential decay of the correlation energy, accompanied by an oscillatory behavior, in both cases with and without the influence of a semiconductor substrate. The comparison with traditional hydrodynamic methods shows that the linearized stochastic approach accurately captures the full-scale hydrodynamic results, in addition to justifying the applicability of the simple quantum hydrodynamic model to a wide range of situations. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrates the significance of non-equilibrium quantum correlations in relation to the decay of the correlation energy. It is also demonstrated that the stochastic approach converges to the same results as the conventional equation of motion for the Wigner function when the simulation time is sufficiently short. The linearized stochastic method offers an efficient and accurate way to study the dynamics of non-equilibrium quantum correlations in semiconductor devices, making it suitable for large-scale simulations. This advancement paves the way for a deeper understanding of the fundamental role of quantum correlations in the dynamics of charge and current in semiconductor devices. As such, it has the potential to guide the further development of these devices. Recent advances in action proposal generation have primarily focused on
sequential models, neglecting inter-frames relationships that are rich in
contextual information. To fill this gap, we introduce the Dual Context
Aggregation Network (DCAN), a non-sequential model that explores contextual
connections across frames through two context aggregation modules with
adaptive weights. By incorporating visual and temporal context for each frame,
DCAN establishes a more comprehensive representation, allowing for precise
detection of actions. Experimental evaluations on the VAO and ActivityNet datasets
reveal that DCAN surpasses the performance of sequential models and serves as a
benchmark for future non-sequential action proposal studies. The code is
available at https://github.com/wh133313/DCAN.

Current methods of evaluating and comparing fuzzers have significant flaws, 
which can lead to misleading conclusions, as they are based on outdated 
metrics that fail to capture the full potential of modern fuzzers. To address 
these limitations, this study introduces an innovative approach that leverages
mutation analysis to enhance the assessment and comparison of fuzzers. To test 
this new framework, the researchers conduct an exhaustive comparison of leading 
fuzzers, including Chandler, ChenSaltFuzz, and honggfuzz, among others, to 
determine their effectiveness in covering more reachable statements in the code. 
Notably, this study finds that Chandler and ChenSaltFuzz exhibit similar levels of 
performance, with both reaching up to 75% coverage of reachable code paths, 
outperforming the traditional metric of fault frequencies under specific test 
conditions. Furthermore, the researchers observe that Chandler's ability to cover 
more code paths is matched by its ability to introduce mutations, which is not 
the case with ChenSaltFuzz. To facilitate replication and advancement of this 
research, the analysis data and associated tools are made publicly available. 
This study offers an optimal approach for conducting comprehensive comparisons 
of fuzzers and is poised to propel the further development of the field. 

Our results indicate that the leading fuzzers can cover up to 75% of reachable code paths.
Our data and evaluation tools are available at https://evalfuzz.com.

When assessing the performance of classification models using randomly generated training and testing sets, the variability in results can be significant. To mitigate this, a new approach called J-K-fold cross validation was introduced by selecting J times K subsets of data for model training. The goal of this method is to determine if J-K-fold cross validation yields more stable performance estimates compared to the standard K-fold cross validation technique. To achieve this goal, models were randomly generated and tested using both standard K-fold and J-K-fold cross validation on artificially generated and real life data. The results showed that J-K-fold cross validation performs better than standard K-fold cross validation especially when the number of data sets (J) is smaller than the number of parameters of the model. It was also found that J needs to be at least 5 times the number of parameters to achieve some level of stability and that this requires a specific form of the model. Ultimately, the study suggests that when working with random data sets, standard K-fold cross validation is adequate. However, when working with real life data, it is recommended to use the number of observations (N) instead of the number of parameters (K) for K in J-K-fold cross validation. Additionally, it was observed that the optimal value of J is reached more quickly with complex models. In such cases, using standard K-fold cross validation may be sufficient. It is also argued that the optimal value of J is reached more quickly with models that have a higher capacity to fit the noise in the data. It is therefore suggested that models which exhibit similar or better performance than the baseline model should be selected for J-K-fold cross validation. It is also recommended to use a minimum of 5 times the number of parameters for J and that this requires a specific form of the model. It is further suggested that when working with real life data, standard K-fold cross validation is adequate and that J should be equal to the number of observations. It is also found that complex models benefit more from J-K-fold cross validation than simple models and that the optimal value of J is reached more quickly with complex models. It is therefore suggested that standard K-fold cross validation can be used for simple models. It is also found that models which exhibit similar or better performance than the baseline model should be selected for J-K-fold cross validation. It is also found that the optimal value of J is reached more quickly with models that have a higher capacity to fit the noise in the data. Recently, research on Teacher-Student architectures has successfully enabled lightweight student networks to match the high performance of deep teacher networks in video action recognition tasks. This has significant implications for the implementation of video action recognition systems on resource-constrained devices. In order to fully leverage the capabilities of Teacher-Student architectures, it is essential to conduct in-depth analysis of the internal working mechanisms and to identify key factors that contribute to their success. In this study, we investigate the effects of various Teacher-Student training configurations, including different training objectives, network types, and extraction frame durations, on the performance of the student network. Our analysis indicates that the primary goal of the teacher network should be to minimize the cross-entropy loss with the student's probability distribution, rather than other objectives such as classification accuracy or total loss. Moreover, our results show that the student network's performance is highly sensitive to the type of network used by the teacher, and that using a teacher network with the same structure as the student can lead to the student failing to learn new knowledge. Additionally, our analysis reveals that extracting information from a larger number of frames does not necessarily improve the student's performance and may even worsen it, and that using temporal aggregation techniques can significantly enhance the student's performance. Our research provides valuable insights into the working mechanisms of Teacher-Student architectures and can serve as a guide for the implementation of video action recognition systems on resource-constrained devices. To address this limitation, we propose the BE-PZO (Bucket Elimination - Progressive Zechner ordering) algorithm, which aims to find a suitable ordering within BE's existing parameter space. Through extensive testing on various real-world applications, our results show that BE-PZO consistently yields orderings that significantly improve inference and optimization performance compared to random ordering. Notably, BE-PZO outperforms the established progressive elimination ordering (PEO) strategy in multiple scenarios. The paired-permutation test is an efficient statistical method for comparing two groups based on paired observations. By treating the difference in data as a random variable, determining its probability distribution and subsequently assessing the significance, this test provides valuable insights. Despite the simplicity of this test, calculating its exact probability distribution proves to be a challenging task. To address this, we developed an exact algorithm for calculating the paired-permutation test, which we discovered is equivalent to a Union-Find algorithm. In addition, we analyzed the performance of this exact algorithm in relation to approximate methods, particularly Monte Carlo simulations, which we found to be significantly more efficient with comparable accuracy. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between test power and the number of permutations used, which we found to be directly proportional. Additionally, we explored the implementation of this test using a data parallelism approach with TensorFlow, which we successfully applied to real-world datasets. Our results indicate that the exact algorithm is substantially more efficient than approximate methods, with the ability to handle large datasets with ease. We also found that the data parallelism approach with TensorFlow offers excellent scalability with only a marginal decrease in efficiency. To facilitate the use of this test, we developed a Python implementation, which is freely available for public use. Through our work, we aim to provide researchers with an efficient and easily accessible tool for conducting the paired-permutation test. This implementation will enable researchers to easily conduct the test on their own datasets, which is demonstrated through an accompanying R package and examples included in our code repository. This allows anyone to easily run the test and reproduce our results. This code is particularly relevant to our previous study, which highlighted the relationship between speech rate and speech comprehension in individuals with normal hearing. This implementation will enable future replication and extension of this research. This study examines how shipping cartels broke down from 2009 to 2018 using data from
Wilsall Shipping Consultants. A collective variable and a network approach were used
to analyze the structure of shipping cartels. Our results show that the number of dominant
shipping cartels decreased from 13 to 5 over the specified period. We then created
a theoretical model to simulate the behavior of shipping companies within this network.
We found that freight rates and shipping quantities were affected by the breakdown of
shipping cartels, with increases of 43.6% and 18.5% respectively in the long run.
Our analysis suggests that the breakdown of shipping cartels contributed to higher freight
rates and increased shipping quantities in the past. However, our results indicate that
these increases were not substantial enough to be the primary drivers of higher freight
rates and shipping quantities over time. Other factors must therefore be given more
consideration. We also verified that our model's results align with actual freight rate and
shipping quantity data. Finally, we identified two critical events that had a major impact
on the breakdown of shipping cartels: the 2011 Arab Spring and the 2015-2016 global shipping
downturn. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the structure
and behavior of shipping cartels and can be applied to analyze similar phenomena in other
industries and markets. Our methodology is openly available to facilitate replication
and further research by other scholars. Our analysis can also benefit shipping companies,
freight brokers, and other industry stakeholders in their decision-making processes.

A loom in the context of Permutahedral topology, is a structured arrangement incorporating various pathological spaces including the Menger and Higuchi wedges, as well as the Nagata-Czyzowski cube. Notably, every loom's structure can be represented by means of a Delaunay triangulation, which in itself is a distinguishing topological feature. In this study, we establish that this characteristic triangulation can be constructed not only within the loom space, but also within any subsequent extension of the loom, which is in turn comprised of the original loom and its subsequent self-retraction. Furthermore, this finding enables us to prove that these self-retractions, in fact, re-create the loom's underlying structure, resulting in a homeomorphism with a corresponding sub-space of an extended loom. As a result, we are able to demonstrate a non-trivial, self-retracting structure that gives rise to a more complex topological space, which in this case is an extended loom space. This breakthrough answers a long-standing question initially posed by B. Borsuk. Additionally, this discovery allows us to exhibit a homeomorphism between certain, intricately related spaces within the loom structure, which is then utilized to solve a variant of the classic Borsuk-Czyzowski problem. Lastly, this study also reveals that any space within the loom family can be perfectly replicated through a process of repeated self-retraction and re-creation, which in turn is driven by a specific type of continuous map, which we have termed the 'loom map'. This understanding we believe will further aid in the exploration of the loom family's topology. Lastly, we outline a strategy that could be employed to explore the properties of the loom space as a whole. This strategy is centered around developing a more refined analysis of the loom space's structure, which in turn is based on a more detailed examination of the properties of its constituent sub-s_spaces, which in this case would involve the Nagata-Czyzowski cube and the Menger wedge. This approach we believe will also be beneficial in addressing other related topological questions. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently achieved remarkable success in tackling complex tasks on structured data. Despite this success, the underlying factors that influence GNNs' predictive ability from both data and algorithmic perspectives remain poorly understood. In this study, we present an extensive analysis of three public datasets to uncover how graph characteristics, node attributes, and GNN architectures impact performance. Our findings indicate that graph structure plays a more significant role than node features in GNNs and suggest certain graph features that contribute to GNNs' ability to generalize. We also examine the effects of node degrees, expansion and convergence rates on GNNs' performance and observe that self-connection can facilitate message passing but may lead to instability in some cases. To address these issues, we propose a novel GNN architecture called Node-Aggregated Graph Neural Network (NAGNN) that incorporates node attributes through an aggregation operation, leading to improved performance on two of the three datasets considered. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of this approach, and we provide theoretical insights into NAGNN's behavior using a simple case study. Source code for NAGNN is available online at this link: https://github.com/ghulame/NAGNN. This work lays the groundwork for a comprehensive study of GNNs that can be useful for practitioners aiming to leverage GNNs on similar structured data tasks.

This paper investigates the geometries associated with singular compact area minimizers in a variety of settings, including both smooth and discontinuous cases, building on previous research by Simons, Scheeffer, and Ros-Sarfaraz. We particularly focus on applying surgery style arguments to better understand these associated geometries. Through this approach, we are able to establish new links between the compact singular areas and associated geometries, even in situations where multiple singular points are present. This enables us to obtain new regularity results for compact singular areas in a variety of settings. For example, in a smooth boundary setting, we have shown that in a neighborhood of a set of smooth singular points with a certain dimension, the set itself can be characterized by a collection of smooth curves. Similarly, in a discontinuous boundary setting, we have demonstrated that the geometry associated with compact singular areas does not contain any flat components. Finally, we have also established a connection between compact singular areas and associated geometries in a multiple singular points case, which provides a crucial groundwork for solving Plateau's problem in a more general context.

Additionally, they found that the entropy in the vortex core follows a specific power law when the temperature is raised, while the entropy associated with the moving magnetic flux line remains constant at higher temperatures. These findings were observed in a number of different materials and are consistent with theoretical predictions made through the use of a Larkin-Ovchinnikov model. The results indicate that high-entropy states in superconductors can be created through the movement of coupled magnetic flux lines and that these states can be distinguished by looking at the entropy in the vortex core. Lastly, researchers were able to use these findings to develop a new method for measuring the flux-line mass in superconductors. The experimental technique used in this study has the potential to be applied to a number of different types of condensed-matter systems in which the motion of a defect can create a high-entropy state, such as magnetic domain walls in ferromagnets or soliton cores in superfluids. We analyzed 20 popular technical indicators, considering factors like simplicity, effectiveness, and correlation with each stock's unique behavior. This optimized subset significantly outperformed both the baseline model and a random selection of indicators. Our study's findings can serve as a foundation for further exploration and enhancement of technical analysis and prediction methods in stock trading. We explore the connection between the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) and the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT), using the unitary gauge choice for the Higgs field. This allows us to analyze double Higgs production in the LHC and future colliders, focusing on beyond-SM Higgs interactions. We find that constraints from the SMEFT parameter space can be obtained using data from the LHC at 13 TeV and the LHC at 100 TeV, which would significantly improve the limits on leading coefficients of dimension-five and six operators affecting double Higgs production. These improvements would lead to more stringent limits on certain HEFT operator coefficients in the double Higgs production channel. Furthermore, we find that future LHC runs and certain HEFT scenarios may be probed to an accuracy of 0.001-0.01% in the leading coefficient of the dimension-five operator when considering the impact of NNLO QCD corrections. Additionally, we investigate the influence of NNLO QCD corrections on the double Higgs production cross-section in the SMEFT/HEFT and compare it to the NNLO QCD prediction for the standard SM HH production process. These studies will help inform the theoretical precision required for a comprehensive analysis of double Higgs production in the SMEFT/HEFT framework at future colliders.

We re-examine the perturbative construction of a parametrized gravitational boundary Hamiltonian model, modifying the decoupling method to split the Einstein equations into two independent sets of differential equations. This modification allows us to efficiently compute boundary observables by bypassing the need to solve the full Einstein equations. Utilizing a conformally flat spacetime and imposing specific boundary conditions, we derive an effective semi-holonomic differential equation governing the time evolution of metric fields near the boundary. We then establish an explicit formula for a particular boundary observable, and through numerical simulations, demonstrate the convergence of our algorithm. Finally, we analyze the implications of our approach on the dynamics of the system near the boundary.

To address this issue, we introduce SceneGen, a method that generates and simulates scenes from a set of given conditions in a single, unified framework. Building on SceneGen, we developed a technique to model traffic scenes in a way that's both accurate and efficient. This approach involves breaking down scene generation into two tasks: modeling the positions and types of objects, and refining the scene for better visibility and realism. By doing so, we show that SceneGen can accurately model object distributions and movements in a real-world environment, and that its derivatives are sufficient to guide a simulation. With this approach, we were able to train a self-driving vehicle to navigate a variety of scenarios in the virtual world, and then successfully test it in the real world. Our results demonstrate that SceneGen can generate scenes that can be safely navigated by self-driving vehicles, and that its derivatives are useful for improving visibility and realism. We're developing a single-code platform that integrates multiple physical processes to create a comprehensive model for the evolution of massive molecular clouds. In this study, we apply this code to an idealized representation of a massive molecular cloud, which gives birth to a cluster of high-mass stars, and observe the development of superbubbles, dust formation, and supernovae explosions within the cloud for approximately one million years. Our integrated network of stars, gas, and dust tracks the movement of supernovae, pair-instability supernovae, core-collapse supernovae, and dust grain formation and evolution, as well as the effects of supernovae on stellar evolution and dust return to the gas. With this approach, we're able to simulate the creation of dust from stellar winds and supernovae explosions and follow dust and gas as they separate within the superbubbles. The model allows us to investigate interactions between stars and the surrounding gas and dust, producing more realistic stellar evolution and predicting various observational indicators such as mass-loss rates, dust creation, and supernovae frequencies. By comparing our results to observations of the Eagle Nebula (M16), specifically with respect to the super-bubble structure and star formation regions, our study highlights the significance of considering the effects of supernovae on stellar evolution and dust return to gas, dust formation from stellar winds and supernovae explosions, and dust and gas separation within superbubbles. To address the challenging task of detecting remote objects on the road, a combined approach is proposed that effectively integrates traditional computer vision and lidar-based methods through shared features. By leveraging the strengths of both techniques, the proposed system achieves superior performance in far-field 3D object detection compared to individual method benchmarks. Specifically, with the use of an efficient neural network architecture, the proposed system surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques on the Waymo Open Dataset benchmark, yielding significant improvements in mean average precision and mean average precision at IOU 0.5 for cars and pedestrians respectively, thus validating the effectiveness of the approach. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be robust in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by results on the Baidu Apollo: Autonomous Driving Dataset. The system's ability to incorporate both RGB and lidar-based detection methods is also analyzed through performance metrics and visualizations, revealing the potential for further optimization and metric learning techniques to enhance object detection accuracy. Additionally, in exploration of system design, a lidar-only system is proposed with an innovative multi-head network architecture, achieving notable detection performance while emphasizing the importance of method robustness in order to prevent overfitting. The system's code is made publicly available on GitHub.

A newly developed linear combination of Gaussian states model, called the linear response generator, can efficiently create complex quantum states on a potential energy surface. This model, which only requires a training set of energies and related derivatives for a small set of input variables, can prepare highly accurate quantum states through an easy-to-implement linear transformation of input Gaussian functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by generating excited states of malonaldehyde using a training set of only three molecules. The results show improved correlation energies and transition probabilities with oscillation amplitudes that match theoretical values, highlighting the potential of this model for use in dynamical processes. Additionally, we find that the number of trainable parameters has a clear connection to the number of training states, and that the linear response generator can be an invaluable tool for designing new chemical systems by identifying critical oscillatory modes. This raises the possibility of applying this model to a broader range of molecules and systems. This work is an important step towards creating a chemical dynamics simulator that can handle large numbers of atomic degrees of freedom and multiple electronic states. This will enable the simulation of complex molecular reactions that involve multiple reference states and large amplitude vibrations, leading to a more accurate and efficient simulation of chemical reactions. This will be achieved by combining the linear response generator with a constrained dynamics approach, such as the one proposed by Tully. This will involve developing a method for training the model that considers multiple reference states, and integrating this model into a full nonadiabatic dynamics simulator. This will involve developing a new massively parallel Monte Carlo trajectory generator that can be trained from experimental data. This will enable the simulation of chemical reactions that can be compared directly to experimental results. This will be particularly useful for predicting and designing new chemical reactions, and will be demonstrated with the prediction of a specific reaction involving a certain molecule. This work has significant implications for the development of chemical dynamics simulators and could potentially be applied to other types of systems and processes. This could involve exploring the potential of this model to be used with other types of Gaussian functions, such as the ones used in the diagonalization of the Feschbach Hamiltonian, and considering alternative approaches to constraining the number of parameters. This could also involve applying this model to other types of chemical systems, such as polymers and clusters, and considering whether the linear response generator could be used in machine learning contexts outside of chemistry. This could raise interesting questions about the potential applications and limitations of this model, and could potentially lead to the development of new chemical dynamics simulators and machine learning models.

We've developed a novel method to align 3D organ models with intraoperative ultrasound data, using a non-rigid transformation and a data-driven approach that's resistant to certain types of errors, such as misaligned and missing data. Unlike traditional methods that rely on optimization techniques, our approach uses a data-driven strategy that's based on probabilistic models and can handle the uncertainties inherent in intraoperative data. We've tested our method with ultrasound data used for guiding surgeries for liver and kidney tumors, and our results show that it's possible to achieve accurate registrations even when the data is noisy, and our method compares favorably to conventional techniques. Our approach also offers a useful tool for validating ultrasound data and identifying areas where the data is unreliable. Furthermore, we've found that it can facilitate the transfer of learning from high-quality preoperative MRI scans to intraoperative ultrasound data. Our code is available online for other researchers to use.

While self-supervised flow estimation has made significant progress in recent years, there remains a persistent issue with occlusions that significantly impede the learning process. To mitigate this limitation, we are proposing a novel self-supervised approach, namely Contrastive Squeeze-Merge (CSM), that incorporates a bidirectional suppression mechanism to counter the effects of occlusions. By leveraging both forward and reverse flow information, our approach refines the feature representation, resulting in a more distinct and overlapping-free representation of the input image. By training CSM using patch-based contrastive learning, we have achieved notable improvements in self-supervised flow estimation performance, with results showing a considerable reduction in error rates of around 5-10% in various benchmark datasets. Notably, our method exhibits improved robustness in handling significant occlusions with a precision rate of over 90% in the Make Flow dataset. Comprehensive analyses, including ablation studies and visualizations, have validated the effectiveness of our bidirectional suppression strategy and contrastive learning approach. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and methodology publicly available. Through enhanced performance and novel insights, our CSM framework has significant potential to propel future self-supervised flow estimation research.

Deep neural networks have significantly outperformed traditional machine learning methods in various signal processing applications, including those involving finite precision. Nonetheless, their complex structure and substantial power demands hinder their utilization in battery-powered devices. To overcome this limitation, a simple, high-performance classifier called the General Purpose Classifier (GPC) is proposed here. Based on a comprehensive evaluation, the GPC's superiority to advanced neural networks is demonstrated. The GPC's performance is on par with Annular Neural Networks (ANNs) in multiple assessment scenarios, including both training and testing modes, without consuming any additional computational resources. The proposed GPC's architecture is subsequently analyzed using the ANNs framework and its circuit implementation is described in detail. To validate the proposed GPC, several classification scenarios are explored and compared to ANNs and other baseline methods. The findings from these experiments provide compelling evidence for the GPC's viability as a reliable, power-efficient classifier. The proposed GPC's code is freely accessible online for the benefit of the signal processing community.
