Three commonly abused psychiatric medications - benzodiazepines, opioids, and sedatives - exhibit significant correlations in their consumption patterns across various regions. To investigate the spatial effects of these correlations, we utilize a geographic expansion of the Multivariate Autoregressive Model. We evaluate the performance of this model using real-world data sets of prescription transactions from British Columbia, Canada. To handle the varying time series lengths across different regions, we apply the technique of equalizing time series lengths through interpolation. We compare different interpolation methods, including a novel one based on the characteristics of time series data, to determine their impact on error estimation. The results indicate that the geographic Multivariate Autoregressive Model yields lower errors than its non-spatial counterpart and provides error estimates that reflect the temporary and permanent effects of regional variations. Furthermore, an analysis of Residual Time Series reveals that there are unmodeled factors influencing consumption patterns approximately every 6-12 months. To facilitate easy access, we create interactive visualizations for the data and estimated parameters, along with a publicly available R package to accommodate user-defined datasets. Previous studies have demonstrated that neural models are capable of learning from labeled semantic relations and can be trained on specific relation types to improve performance on semantic relation classification tasks. However, these models are yet to fully exploit the hierarchical structure of relations implicit in conditional statements (i.e., if A, then B) that reflect general logical rules. In this study, we examine the potential benefits of training neural models on a hierarchical structure of if-then relations and find that doing so enhances model performance on relation classification tasks, particularly on less common relation types. Furthermore, we investigate approaches to combining hierarchical relations with relation types that share the same antecedent or consequent for training neural models. Experimental results indicate that both methods yield models with better classification performance on unseen data. Interestingly, we find that models trained on hierarchical relations and combination approaches show improved performance on rare relation types and find that the optimal approach depends on the characteristics of the dataset in question. Ultimately, our findings suggest that neural models' ability to learn from labeled semantic relations extends to complex structures like if-then relations and that they are capable of extracting useful information from conditional statements. In doing so, we establish new baseline models and offer theoretical insights that can inform the development of future neural models in this domain. Ultimately, we believe that this study represents a significant step towards a full-fledged formal semantics for deep learning models. All code and models developed as part of this study have been made publicly available online.

This enhanced algorithm incorporates a novel, iterative approach to approximating the inverse of a unitary matrix using only applications of the matrix and its adjoint, and is demonstrated on a scenario involving matrix inversion within the HHL algorithm. Furthermore, we examine various NISQ-HHL configurations and evaluate their performance on actual quantum hardware from IBM and Rigetti, showing that our iterative approach leads to a significantly faster execution on these devices. Notably, on IBM's ibm-qiskit-toronto, we achieve a substantial speedup of approximately $80\times$ for one iteration of the inverse using the phase estimation tool provided by the manufacturer. Transferring learned speech representations to linguistic tasks like speech recognition is challenging due to a limited connection between the two. To address this, we introduce a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) that enables the exchange of context between the two. By incorporating BiAM, a cross-task speech-linguistic encoder with two interconnected encoders is proposed. The BiAM-speech encoder pays attention to both the speech input and the linguistic labels, while the BiAM-linguistic encoder attends to both the encoded speech representations and the input acoustic features. We demonstrate that the proposed BiAM cross-task encoder outperforms the self-supervised encoder and the encoder with a unidirectional attention mechanism on both zero-resource speech recognition and semantic speech recognition tasks. The BiAM cross-task encoder also achieves comparable performance to the multitask encoder on zero-resource speech recognition, while surpassing it on the semantic speech recognition task. The BiAM cross-task encoder facilitates the exchange of context between the speech representations and the linguistic information, thereby alleviating the challenging initial stages of the speech recognition task. Notably, the BiAM cross-task encoder exhibits an attention mechanism that focuses on both the speech input and the linguistic labels equally in order to accurately decode the speech, giving it an advantageous performance over the baseline models. This research introduces a new 3D pose representation and a corresponding neural network framework that uses bidirectional projections to improve viewpoint-invariant video analysis. Unlike existing methods that use single-projection representations, our approach uses both projection directions to create a dual representation. This representation enables efficient boundary loss calculation and reduces overfitting in deep neural networks. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed dual representation significantly outperforms single-projection representations in accuracy and is particularly effective in predicting novel viewpoints, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin of 8.4%. This improvement supports the hypothesis that high-eccentricity viewpoints are learned more effectively when using the dual representation. The proposed approach also enhances robustness against lighting variations and facial expression changes in videos. Notably, our results indicate that dual-softmax baselines already exhibit better performance than several non-dual boundary loss baselines in various evaluation metrics. The code for this research is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zh11627021991/DeepCap-DSM. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the Computer Vision Foundation (CVF) workshops on Human Workshop and Face Workshops in 2022. The evaluation protocol is based on the work of Voulodimos et al. from 2018 and the DeepCap dataset from 2020. The proposed approach has applications in video-based single-view 3D face reconstruction and can be used to create a variety of morphological maps for analyzing the shape and appearance of faces. This technique has been incorporated into the DeepCap system, a real-time 3D face reconstruction system that utilizes a single RGB video stream. The system has been utilized in multiple real-world scenarios, such as monitoring face temperature elevations and detecting facial skin cancer. The DeepCap system has been made available as a public API at https://deepcap.mikelukas.com/. This paper presents a novel algorithm capable of generating fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space that maintains even face angles. The algorithm adapts the Simplicial Empirical Shape Operator method, originally developed for two-dimensional spaces, with significant modifications. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by creating 25 new fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space. Additionally, this work showcases the first known fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space with specific rotational symmetries missing from the existing Coxeter groups. Furthermore, this research indicates that polyhedra generated by the algorithm can exhibit high internal density. We also introduce a new concept, the Shape Operator Spectrum Decrement, which helps evaluate the simplicity of polyhedra configurations. This study facilitates the exploration of complex polyhedra configurations and sheds light on the construction of fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space. Sequential models, such as tree LST and sequential LST, incorporate local heuristics to capture sentence hierarchy, but their reliance on hierarchy is less clear. Our analysis reveals that these models leverage hierarchy only to some extent and often use local heuristics that are unrelated to the hierarchy. Conversely, simple models like BERT and RoBERTa, which are not designed with hierarchy in mind, perform similarly well on multiple evaluations, suggesting that hierarchy is not a crucial feature for understanding sentences. Additionally, our results indicate that the heuristics used by sequential LST are often inconsistent and may be unnecessary, which raises concerns about their applicability to other tasks and potential overfitting. Ultimately, our study implies that LST's ability to comprehend sentence structure is an area in need of further research and paves the way for exploring non-hierarchical sentence representations.

To accurately model this signal, we utilize the MadGraph 5 interface to compute next-to-leading order cross sections and combine them with leading logarithmic resummation through the Effective Field Theory of the Vector Boson Distribution (vBFFET). To validate the accuracy of our implementation, we compare the results to explicit calculations of irreducible semi-leptonic decays obtained using MadGraph 5/Pythia 8. To make the most of future LHC data, we also investigate the sensitivity of the relevant reconstruction channels to the mass of the vector leptoquarks. For this, we will provide the reconstruction efficiency and cross section as a function of the vector leptoquark mass to facilitate adjustments to the experimental analysis. A recent deep-neural-network (DNN) approach known as low-dose PET-MRI combined deep consistency prior (LdDCP) has demonstrated its capacity to create high-quality low-dose PET images utilizing MRI data from the same anatomical location, with the assistance of an additional consistency layer. However, the LdDCP model's ability to utilize MRI information in the transaxial direction may be limited by its use of the encoder, which applies convolutional layers. Furthermore, using the encoder's output for each image slice also results in the model having access to information from adjacent slices, which may contaminate the expected output of the LdDCP model during training. To address these issues, we propose an alternative framework called the low-dose PET-MRI combined deep consistency prior (ldDCP), which uses two separate encoders for each individual image slice, utilizing MRI data from the entire field-of-view (FOV) without any-dimensional low-pass filtering. Our experimental results indicate that the ldDCP approach not only outperforms the LdDCP model but also yields comparable performance to that of an iterative expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm while requiring significantly fewer iterations and producing more realistic images than a non-linear EM (NLEM) algorithm, which serves as the benchmark for low-dose PET image reconstruction algorithms. Moreover, the proposed ldDCP approach outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning networks, including U-Net and a CNN with bilateral loss, in terms of both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ldDCP model can effectively utilize MRI data from the same anatomical location to enhance the quality of low-dose PET images, as well as leverage MRI information in the transaxial direction to improve the accuracy of pixel values. Lastly, we validate the generalizability of the ldDCP approach across various types of PET and MRI modalities by successfully applying it to a different dataset while only making minimal adjustments to the training parameters. Notably, the ldDCP approach exhibits superior performance even when compared to high-resolution PET images used in conjunction with low-resolution MRI images, which serves as a more challenging and clinically relevant scenario. Lastly, we explore the potential of the ldDCP approach to handle multiple imaging modalities and present several potential research directions for this novel framework. All code and data used in this study are available online for replication purposes.

Our results indicate that the models with fully contextualized modules have a higher coreference accuracy and a more accurate relation to centering theory than the linear model. We also observe that the models with fully contextualized modules have a different distribution of centering accuracy in relation to discourse status than the linear model. Our findings suggest that contextualized embeddings play a key role in the improved coreference resolution models and support further research into the relationship between contextualized embeddings, centering theory, and coreference resolution. We also propose a method for analyzing the contextualized embeddings in these models. Our analysis and proposed method can be used to study other language models in relation to centering theory and coreference. Our study is available online at https://github.com/AlaaMidigy/CT-COREF. Previous methods that use learning algorithms to determine system settings from user feedback have been focused solely on optimizing system performance metrics, without considering the human understanding of system configurations. We propose a new approach, guided configuration learning, that involves optimizing both performance and human understandability in system settings. This is achieved by incorporating a human-related cost function into the optimization process, allowing us to derive a closed-form solution for optimal system configurations using an inverse method. We evaluate our approach through both theoretical and practical analyses, using two case studies - one involving user feedback on search engine results pages (SERPs), and the other on personalized news article recommendations. Our results show that guided configuration learning outperforms both traditional optimization methods and learning algorithms that do not consider human understandability. In the SERPs case study, we found that optimizing human understandability reduces search time by 26%, while in the news article case study, we found that guided configuration learning improves human understandability by 88% and reduces the human-related cost by 74%. We also observed that incorporating human understandability into the cost function has a 1.37 times greater impact on system performance than providing 50% more relevant results. Finally, we found that guided configuration learning can be applied to large-scale systems, including online platforms, by leveraging distributed optimization algorithms. We publicly release our code and datasets for both case studies.

A new algorithm is presented, based on a cycle consistent deep learning technique, to use a lot of data with associated geospatial coordinates to learn a transformation to map estimated locations to actual locations. In the context of the Rendezvous Scenario, where two advanced civilizations meet, we examine the energy sources that could be most beneficial for them to share. Considering five possible energy forms - M-brane energy, dark energy, dark matter energy, M87* energy similar to that of Ultramassive Black Holes, and the energy within Neutron Star or White Dwarf batteries - we assess their availability, feasibility, and effectiveness in the encounter. It is determined that the most versatile and useful energy source for the meeting is the energy within Neutron Star or White Dwarf batteries, as it can be easily harnessed and provided in any desired amount. This source of energy enables the possibility of recharging energy batteries during the encounter, making it the most suitable for the meeting's energy needs. This finding also implies that if a meeting is taking place near an ULHB, such as M87*, it is likely to occur over a wide range of distances, up to a few billion parsecs, due to the strong energy output from such a location drawing the meeting spot towards it. This, in turn, could result in the approach of the meeting spot being in the direction of the nearest ULHB, potentially allowing for the detection of such a meeting spot as it moves towards an ULHB. The most suitable energy source for the meeting is further supported by a consideration of the energy needs of different types of civilizations, with Type I civilizations needing all the energy they can get, Type II civilizations being able to manage a large amount of energy, and Type III, IV, and V civilizations being able to handle any amount of energy. A mathematical model is also developed to estimate the energy that can be extracted from an ULHB, as well as the distance over which it can be effectively used. A numerical analysis of this model yields an energy limit that could be extracted from an ULHB, which is proportional to the square of the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole, specifically in the range of 10^57 to 10^58 GeV, and could be used an an energy reference point. A potential method for the civilizations to use this energy is also considered, along with an estimate of the time it would take to move an asteroid or a planet using this energy. Finally, an examination of an ULHB's energy dynamics, including the energy released by the accretion disk and the movement of the meeting spot, is proposed, along with an opportunity for the detection of the meeting spot as it moves towards an ULHB. A new model incorporating forces due to van der Waals, electrostatic, and gravity proposes that sticking between colliding grains in a solar composition gas occurs at a specific temperature range where the sticking force surpasses the fragmentation force. According to this model, sticking between grains in a molecular hydrogen-rich environment occurs at temperatures below 20 K, and in a highly depleted environment at temperatures up to 40 K. Above these temperatures, increasing heat would cause grains to fragment upon collision. A separate model using a three-body interaction approach also predicts that grain collisions fragment at temperatures greater than 10 K. Both models suggest that grain growth may be facilitated in regions with low temperatures and limited grain growth in highly turbulent environments. A multi-dimensional simulation incorporating the first sticking model finds that grains may grow to meters in size within one to three orbital periods in a highly depleted environment at low temperatures, and also identifies a possible limit to further growth through collisions with smaller grains. A comparison of this model with recent data from ALMA reveals that grains in the HL/T Tauri disk are likely one to two meters in diameter, and a simple estimation suggests that grains in the HH29 jet are around one meter in diameter. Further analysis indicates that the grain size in the HL/T Tauri disk may be constrained by a maximum fragmentation depth due to collision with smaller grains, resulting in a maximum mass growth of one to three solar masses per orbital period. A subsequent analysis of the HL/T Tauri disk's grain size distribution based on the model reveals an index of 2.5, which may be influenced by the distribution of smaller grains. A final analysis of the model suggests that planetesimal formation through grain collision and sticking may occur more efficiently in warmer protoplanetary disks with extremely dry environments, and that further research is needed to better understand how the composition of a protoplanetary disk affects the formation of solid bodies through grain collision and sticking. Constrained imitation learning can effectively address the issues of nonlinear hard constraints in robot skill learning by mimicking trajectories that adhere to established safety guidelines. Despite its potential, this method's broader adoption is hindered by the difficulty of obtaining dense reward signals that align with the constraints. In response, we introduce a new constrained imitation learning framework, Projecting Constraints into Latent (PCIL), which utilizes both self-supervised and supervised learning to develop a robust and precise predictor of constraint violation. This violation predictor is then utilized in a contrastive learning objective that effectively projects the feature space of latent dynamics models in a way that reduces the error in predicting constraint adherence. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that PCIL's dynamic models exhibit more precise and safe generalization on new task instances, particularly when evaluated under uncertain and safety-critical conditions. Most notably, PCIL outperforms baseline methods by displaying the ability to safely generalize to situations that were not encountered during training. As such, PCIL offers a viable solution for the robot skill learning challenge that involves learning from limited labeled data and strict safety constraints. Using unitarity methods and discrete integral equations from the residue theorem for forward amplitudes in QCD, we calculate the two-gluon collinear expansion variable (CEV) in QCD. We then demonstrate that the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory can be determined through a combination of the two-gluon CEV and the ultrasoft limit. Additionally, we find the ultrasoft limit of the six-gluon amplitude to be in agreement with previously derived results based on the BFKL equation. Furthermore, we find that the two-gluon CEV is directly related to the Källén function of the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. This relationship enables us to determine the conformal limit of the Källén function for six-gluon amplitudes in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Our results extend previous findings on the conformal limit of the Källén function for four- and five-guon amplitudes. We also find that the two-gluon collinear limit of the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory is over-determined and that the leading colour amplitude is correctly captured by the colour organised field theory calculation. This leads to the conclusion that the BFKL equation correctly describes the colour structure of the six-gluon amplitude in the leading colour channel. Nevertheless, the BFKL equation fails to account for the leading order colour organisation correctly, and instead, leads to a colour dependence that contradicts unitarity. This discrepancy arises solely from the colour organised treatment of the BFKL equation. If the BFKL kernel is constructed from colour-ordered amplitudes, the colour dependence from the BFKL equation agrees with the colour organised calculation. Finally, we find that the conformal limit of the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory exhibits a symmetry under the exchange of two gluons, providing an independent verification of contact terms used in the calculation of amplitude Graviton exchange in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. We examine the topological characteristics of a specific quantum state found in Sr$_2$MnO$_4$ with a nonmagnetic impurity, considering the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity. A recent study using the Shubnikov--de Haas oscillations technique revealed that Sr$_2$MnO$_4$'s topological state is destroyed by the presence of a nonmagnetic impurity, which is consistent with our theoretical analysis. We demonstrate that the spin-orbit coupling plays a significant role in determining the topological properties of this state and that it is responsible for converting a non-trivial quantum state into a trivial one. Additionally, we found that the presence of a nonmagnetic impurity leads to a shift in the Fermi surface due to the scattering of electrons with opposite spins at the Fermi level, resulting in the breaking of topological protection. This requires an energy higher than the superconducting gap for the appearance of a zero-bias peak in Sr$_2$MnO$_4$. Our study also indicates that the spin-orbit coupling plays a crucial role in the formation of a zero-bobias peak due to the presence of a nonmagnetic impurity. We conclude that Sr$_2$MnO$_4$ is an example of a $p$-wave chiral superconductor, and that the spin-orbit coupling is necessary for the topological nontriviality of its quantum state. This finding is further supported by an analysis of the Berry phase and the topological $Z_2$ invariant. This theoretical framework is applicable to other materials with similar band structures and can be applied to study the topological characteristics of these materials.

The effect of surface curvature on free energy due to stretching in polymer brushes is examined, determining that strong curvature causes the brush to transition back to a compact conformation near the surface, and that the influence of curvature dominates over that of surface tension in certain cases. A mathematical model has been developed, validated through comparison with existing theories, and is further applied to analyze the behavior of polymer brushes on spherical, cylindrical, and planar surfaces under various forces. Simulation results show that strong surface tension can cause a layering effect, where the brush conformation is influenced by the surface's presence even at large distances away from the surface. The model is also used to study the melting temperature of polymer brushes, and it is found that surface curvature has an opposing effect on the melting temperature, either increasing it by reducing the brush's symmetry, or decreasing it by providing a pathway for chain melting. The influence of the brush's melting temperature on its stretching behavior is also examined. The developed model can be further modified to study other properties of polymer brushes by introducing additional forces and adjusting parameters accordingly. The methods employed to solve the equations also offer room for improvement, particularly in relation to the Monte Carlo method used in the study. To effectively discover binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, this study introduces an analytical approach to comparing measured and expected point spread functions in images obtained from space telescopes. Specifically, this work adapts and simplifies the standard technique for analyzing point spread functions by applying it to a large set of images of known asteroids from the Pan-STARRS survey. By analyzing the differences between observed and simulated point spread functions, this study can identify and remove image artifacts, recover lost flux, and estimate measurement uncertainties. Using this approach on a sample of 1.3 million asteroid detections from the Pan-STARRS S1 dataset, this work identified 26 binary asteroid candidates and reported their characteristics. Notably, this study found its results for binary asteroid candidates to be consistent with previous findings, and it suggests that the discovered binaries have sufficiently large orbits to complete a rotation cycle within less than 10 days. Furthermore, this study proposes using orbital elements in addition to absolute magnitude to improve the registration of asteroid systems in catalogs. By doing so, it would allow for more accurate matching of discovered binary or multiple asteroid candidates with existing entries in the catalog. Additionally, this study found its approach to analyzing point spread functions to be an efficient and effective method for detecting binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, and it is particularly beneficial for use with space-based surveys that have low-cost, wide-field cameras similar to the one on the Small Astronomical Telescope for General Education (ASTE). Lastly, this study emphasized the importance of obtaining follow-up observations to confirm the status of detected binary asteroid candidates through orbital analysis and suggested that future surveys should prioritize selecting targets with low thermal emission levels to enhance detection sensitivity for binaries. Ultimately, this study aimed to lay the groundwork for a more systematic approach to discovering binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys. It proposed a strategy that involves analyzing point spread functions, selecting targets with low thermal emission levels, and conducting follow-up observations to confirm detected candidates. By adopting this strategy in future surveys, it would be possible to discover more binary asteroid candidates and shed more light on the presence of small asteroid systems.

Considerable research has been conducted on the extension-driven Gondwana breakup, particularly in western DRC, eastern Angola, and southern Africa.  However, the role of these extensions in forming the African margin of Gondwana has not been well-defined.

In the western DRC and eastern Angola, an inner craton was surrounded by multiple extensional episodes, resulting in a layered sequence of passive margins.  The extensions occurred in different directions and speeds, and there was a significant speed increase during the final extension.

In the Kaapvaal craton, the Vaalbarien craton, and the Kalahari craton in southern Africa, multiple extensions also occurred, but with significantly faster speeds.  The extensions formed several distinct episodes of extension, and the cratons were located at various distances from the African margin of Gondwana.

The findings suggest that the extension direction and speed, as well as how they changed over time, played a crucial role in the formation and development of the marginal cratons during the Gondwana breakup. Studies have shown that incorporating a theory-of-mind (TOM) approach into reinforcement learning from scratch is challenging, if not impossible, with a single agent. This paper investigates whether an agent's ability to infer teammates' intentions enhances its performance in a collaborative game environment. To evaluate this, we created a simple multi-agent scenario using the GridWorld setup, with an agent working towards a goal and avoiding a hazard. The goal can be reached by moving left or right, but only a specific action is safe. Successfully reaching the goal requires considering the agent's own actions as well as those of the teammate. When both agents learned independently using temporal difference learning with external knowledge, there was no significant difference in performance. However, using a simpler method without external knowledge, an agent that could infer its teammate's intentions by learning the teammate's action-values from its own action-values, significantly outperformed baseline methods, achieving a higher success rate in reaching the goal. This suggests that considering a teammate's TOM can lead to better outcomes in collaborative games. Deeply knotted proteins, characterized by complex cross-linking patterns, often fold back on themselves multiple times, making their folding pathways difficult to predict. In contrast, shallowly knotted proteins have a single-point knot and typically fold in a more straightforward manner. In this study, we examine the intermediate category of proteins with multiple shallow knots. Utilizing advanced computational techniques to map potential folding routes, we identify a distinct pattern where these proteins fold in stages, with each shallow knot being created before the entire structure is finalized. Interestingly, the specific folding path for each shallow knot is already predetermined and cannot be altered, despite minor variations allowed by the protein's local dynamics. Our analysis indicates that the deeper knots are generally folded first, with a deeper knot often acting as a catalyst for folding a nearby shallow one. Our research provides valuable insights into the folding mechanisms of proteins with complex structures and highlights the significance of distinguishing between shallow and deep knots. Furthermore, our findings suggest that predicting the folding of deeply knotted proteins may benefit from first identifying the location and structure of the deeply knotted regions. Recent studies in data augmentation have focused on using approximate models to
generate high-quality counterfactual data. Despite achieving success, these models
suffer from an important limitation: they are trained within a fixed functional
space with unknown implications on the efficacy of such models when using new
approximate models to generate data for existing models. This study challenges all
existing views on data augmentation by demonstrating that generating counterfactual
data can actually be beneficial even when using significantly worse approximation
models. We present a novel algorithm called DISCO that allows the approximate
model to differ from the original model and counterfactual data to be mapped
back to the original input space. Utilizing DISCO, we show that training with
such approximate models on counterfactual data yields not only enhanced robustness
and generalization but also a deeper understanding of the underlying data
distribution. Our method also enables us to leverage multiple approximate models
for various downstream tasks, either explicitly or implicitly. Interestingly,
we found that using approximate models that are substantially worse is actually
preferable to using better ones, as demonstrated by our experiments on both
image classification and language modeling. Notably, we achieved improved performance
on a real-world image classification dataset, even when approximating the model
without any additional memory or computational overhead. Our findings also show
that simple neural network approximations can yield superior results to complex
transformer models, explicitly showcasing the efficacy of DISCO in extracting
underlying data patterns. All of our code and models are available at
https://github.com/hayun267/Generalizable-Data-Augmentation. Our paper has been
accepted for publication at NeurIPS 2022.

In multi-label classification, each data point is associated with a group of relevant class labels.  When learning multi-label classification, the target is to predict a probability distribution over all possible class labels, with class relevance indicating whether the label should be generated during inference.  Due to data scarcity and the vast potential number of relevant class labels, generating high-quality multi-label data is extremely challenging.  This study introduces a single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling method to efficiently produce multi-label data with only single-label annotations.  By analyzing the inherent characteristics of multi-label classification, we propose using a latent variable model to sample multiple relevant class labels based on a single anchor label.  The proposed method is simple, flexible, and scalable for large datasets.  Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that the S2M sampling method is an effective data augmentation technique, outperforming traditional data augmentation methods and matching top-performing model performance without additional annotations. We derive the exact closed-form expressions for the first four moments of this distribution and show that they are directly related to the corresponding moments of the underlying asset returns, providing a clear and practical way to interpret the characteristics of cross-sectional stock returns. To illustrate the effectiveness of this model, we conduct empirical analyses using real-world data from the S\&P 500 index and demonstrate that it effectively captures the skewness and kurtosis of actual return distributions across individual stocks. Furthermore, the model allows for a clear examination of the relationship between the cross-sectional distribution of returns and the underlying asset returns, revealing significant variability in returns across individual stocks and a distinct pattern of return distribution for low- and high-pricing stocks. Lastly, the model is applied to answer questions about the effectiveness of portfolio diversification through stock pricing and the impact of low-pricing stocks on portfolio performance. The results highlight the value of the Bessel function distribution as a versatile tool for analyzing cross-sectional stock returns. Recently, significant breakthroughs have been achieved in cardiac abnormality detection using deep learning techniques, with attention-based methods being particularly prominent. Nevertheless, current deep learning models are still prone to errors in noisy medical images. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed that utilizes self-supervised learning from noisy data to improve the robustness of cardiac abnormality detection models. Specifically, the proposed method employs a contrastive learning technique to introduce auxiliary prototypes representative of normal heart conditions from a large noisy dataset, and then incorporates these prototypes into an existing attention-based model as additional prototypes for prototype distortion loss. By fine-tuning the model on a smaller and cleaner dataset, the proposed method is capable of reducing errors in cardiac abnormality detection by approximately 12% when compared to alternative robust training methods. The evaluation of the proposed method, referred to as Cardiac Prototype Distortion (CPD), yielded comparable performance to state-of-the-art attention-based models on two public datasets and notable improvements on two clinical datasets with low and moderate data quality, respectively. Notably, the proposed CPD technique achieves a notable 21% decrease in error rate on a certain low-quality clinical dataset. The code for the proposed CPD technique has been made publicly available on GitHub at the address indicated below. The proposed CPD approach offers a feasible technique for producing robust cardiac abnormality detection models, capable of mitigating noise's adverse impact on detection performance. Consequently, this method has the potential to contribute to the production of more reliable and robust cardiac abnormality detection models. The proposed CPD technique's code can be found at https://github.com/zhengzheng460/CPD. The increasing use of wearable devices for health monitoring has created a surge in activity recognition research using sensor data. While existing methods effectively classify activities for individual users, their limitations become apparent when applied to a broader population. A major constraint is the requirement for extensive training data on each user, making it difficult to apply to new individuals. A recent deep learning approach known as FedHealth has shown promise in addressing this challenge by combining training data from multiple users to classify activities more accurately and efficiently across different subjects. In this research, we evaluate FedHealth's performance under various training and testing scenarios, including classifications of activities for the same subject, different subjects, and a broader population. A comparison of FedHealth's results to alternative methods, such as traditional multivariate methods and DeepLearnomics, reveals that FedHealth yields the highest classification accuracy when testing against new subjects and a broader population. Notably, FedHealth's performance surpasses DeepLearnomics, even when trained and tested on the same subjects, demonstrating its ability to handle complex, unseen data. A visualization of the temporal patterns identified by FedHealth on multiple subjects also highlights its ability to recognize repeating patterns in activity data. Although FedHealth exhibits lower accuracy in classifications of activities for the same subject, likely due to overcomplication of simple decision boundaries, it remains the top-performing method in the study. In conclusion, FedHealth represents a groundbreaking approach to wearable activity recognition, enabling the accurate classification of activities for new subjects and a broader population, and is thus an invaluable tool for health monitoring applications. Furthermore, FedHealth's flexible usage of training data makes it an attractive option for researchers and healthcare professionals seeking to analyze sensor data in various health contexts. To facilitate future research, we have made available the code and datasets used in this analysis.

We address the challenge of selecting the best differential equation model to fit epidemiological data by using a Bayesian approach and the Monte Carlo method. This approach involves evaluating multiple models simultaneously, which significantly increases computational demands when using traditional methods. To improve performance, we simplify the problem by limiting model variations to realistic Scenarios, which are then compared for accuracy in capturing the dynamics of disease spread. In our case study, we apply this approach to data from the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in Portugal, considering factors such as migration, travel restrictions, and vaccination. Results showing the implications of these interventions on epidemiological parameters are currently being analyzed to differentiate their effects in the portuguese scenario. This method enables policymakers to make informed decisions about control measures by modeling the effects of these interventions on the spread of the disease. Furthermore, our method facilitates the identification of critical events that significantly impact the epidemiological curve, such as the start of vaccination, by comparing model trajectories with actual data. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of Bayesian Monte Carlo methods in evaluating complex dynamic models, addressing a common issue in epidemiological modeling where the true dynamics may be distorted by various factors, including those that are difficult to model, such as individual behavior. This approach provides a solution to the classic problem of model selection by enabling the simultaneous comparison of different models, which is essential for fitting epidemiological data with scratch dynamics. This work is an extension of our previous research presented at the 2021 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control, now including additional methods for evaluating models and a new approach for modeling vaccination campaigns. This paper offers a self-contained overview, incorporating fresh technique for assessment and a case study on Portugal's COVID-19 data, in addition to revised analysis and new findings. In this research, we examine how primer pair design influences storage organization by dividing DNA strands into distinct sections.  We developed a new algorithm that selects primer pairs based on data content, allowing for more efficient storage usage.  Our results show our approach leads to better storage performance, particularly in scenarios with limited read operations, and can choose primer pairs that store data in multiple sections.  We also found our method has potential applications in other DNA storage systems that manage data access through primer pairs.  Our findings were validated through both theoretical and practical testing, and showed our primer pair design can result in better storage usage and reduce storage costs.  We openly share our primer pair design algorithm and matching read operations strategy in the community for further development and use in future DNA data storage systems.  We also outline directions for future research, such as integrating our primer pair design with other DNA storage system components, and explore ways to improve storage performance through additional storage technologies. We have discovered a novel class of solid-state systems, based on a Euclidean lattice, that exhibit nodal lines in momentum space. These specific systems, described by a tight-binding model, feature isolated rings or three-dimensional curves without a clear direction, that are absent in real space. Unlike other topological states, nodal lines are unique in that they do not wrap around the Brillouin zone or form points or lines in real space. Those based on a honeycomb lattice can be transformed into a Weyl semimetal by changing a hopping parameter, while those based on a square lattice can be converted into a topological insulator by altering a different hopping parameter. We propose that these systems could be realized experimentally using a graphene lattice with a zigzag pattern and a hexagonal lattice with armchair pattern, and that they offer a platform for studying nodal lines. Additionally, we predict that they should display signatures in their optical conductivity and dielectric function. We also suggest possible experimental identification methods, including through the analysis of angular momentum, fermi surface anisotropy, and topological charges. We further propose that these systems could be used to produce unique optical responses and that they offer a potential platform for studying topological effects in angular momentum dependent interactions. We simulate these systems using ab initio methods and find good agreement with our predictions. We also find that one of the systems displays a large anomalous Hall effect when doped. We hope that these findings will lead to the experimental identification of these systems and the study of their topological properties. A multi-task Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model was developed and
its variations tested to evaluate its performance on identifying and outlining
various brain tumors. The primary focus was on classifying and outlining
Meningioma, Glioma, and Malignant tumors, as well as detecting and outlining
a tumor in brain scans. The developed model was trained using the
BrainTumorsDataset, a collection of magnetic resonance brain scans featuring
tumors in three different imaging perspectives. The dataset comprises 4
image types and a total of 200 brain scans, divided into training sets of
160 images and testing sets of the remaining 40 images. The developed CNN
model was trained using the Keras platform with the support of U-Net, a
high-performing CNN architecture renowned for its outstanding results in
segmenting and outlining medical images. The model consisting of four
layers was trained with various combinations of layer types, such as
BatchNormalization, Dropout, and ReLU, to determine which structure
yields the highest accuracy in tumor classification and outlining. The test
results showed an average accuracy of 73.33% in classifying brain tumors and
an average outline accuracy of 75.5% in outlining tumors from brain scans. 
The research revealed that the inclusion of pre-training and data
augmentation boosted the model's performance by 10% in tumor outlining and
68.33% in tumor classification. The highest accuracy achieved in the
experiment was 86.67% in tumor outlining and 73.33% in tumor classification. 
The research may contribute to the evolution of medical imaging technology
by providing alternatives to the recurrent CNN models, which are typically
employed in multi-slice image segmentation tasks. The source code for the
model is available for replication on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdullahAlfarisi/Brain-Tumor-Classification.

Our research shows that such LUTs are highly compact, with manageable sizes, and can be employed to compute accurate shadows for various lighting scenarios, including complex environments and dynamic objects. Recently, deep convolutional neural networks have achieved notable success in video deinterlacing tasks, surpassing the performance of traditional methods. A well-structured training approach and careful network design are key factors contributing to this improvement. Nevertheless, the current technique has one significant drawback - it requires both horizontal and vertical scan paths as input, which is not always available in real-world applications. In this research, we introduce a one-dimensional DCNN called S-DACNN, which processes interlaced video frames utilizing a single scan path. The proposed model leverages spatial and temporal information from the scan path to enhance deinterlacing quality. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model performs comparably to state-of-the-art techniques utilizing both scan paths, while also exhibiting adaptability across various video content types. Moreover, the proposed model excels in real-world applications, as demonstrated by its efficacy in compressing and editing interlaced videos. The developed network has the added benefit of being efficient in terms of computational requirements. The trained model weighs approximately 13MB, making it suitable for a variety of applications requiring low latency and memory usage. To facilitate online estimation of riverbed bathymetry from flow velocity measurements, we propose a principal component geostatistical approach (PCGA). PCGA combines the ability of Gaussian processes to handle diverse data types with the efficiency of using flow simulation models to update parameters. Specifically, PCGA utilizes a spatial factor analysis model to represent the bed elevations as a limited number of principal components, whose values can be estimated from flow velocity measurements at multiple points. We leverage the efficiency of flow simulation models to update the parameters of this representation, replacing the need for an inverse problem solver. This approach allows for near-real-time estimation of bathymetry from flow velocity measurements, which is demonstrated using data from the Isabella experiment. The results show that PCGA can accurately estimate bathymetry, even with significant changes in flow conditions, and that the method is robust to the choice of hyperparameters. We also compare PCGA to traditional Gaussian process regression and flow simulation models used individually, showing that PCGA provides a more efficient and accurate way to estimate bathymetry from flow velocity measurements. Additionally, we investigate the ability of PCGA to handle data from different flow regimes and sensors, which is critical for its application in real-world settings. We also examine the scalability of PCGA to larger domains and suggest ways to improve its performance in such cases. The implementation of PCGA is made available online for researchers to use and adapt the method for their own applications. The code is compatible with the popular Python libraries Xarray, Dask, and Scipy, and is easily adaptable to a parallel computing environment using Dask. Creating HDR images from multiple low-resolution images captured using an auto-exposure camera is a complex process. The auto-exposure setting for each image affects the HDR reconstruction, and improper settings can result in poor-quality HDR images. This paper introduces an automatic exposure detection system that uses a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to classify exposure settings from a single HDR image. The proposed system is efficient, user-friendly, and simple to integrate with existing HDR reconstruction methods. By leveraging this system, we developed an automated HDR reconstruction approach that detects exposure settings and uses them to construct HDR images. This system was tested with various HDR reconstruction methods and demonstrated significant improvements in CRF and PSNR scores, with results comparable to those obtained with manually adjusted exposure settings. Notably, our automated system outperformed existing automatic exposure detection methods and proved particularly effective with limited training data. The proposed system's efficiency and performance with only 16 training images per category make it an attractive solution for use in real-world applications. This leads to enhanced HDR image quality when compared to conventional HDR reconstruction approaches and demonstrates the method's potential to be trained on one category and fine-tuned on another. This research analyzes the performance of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner for solving iterative linear systems arising from the discretization of elliptic partial differential equations. The study considers a general, non-uniform coarse space and examines the implicit treatment of inexact solvers within the BDDC framework. The analysis provides specific conditions on the BDDC parameters that guarantee its optimal $O(nz^2)$ or near-optimal $O(nz)$ complexity, where $n$ represents the number of degrees of freedom and $z$ signifies the number of subdomains. The research also explores the impact of inexact solvers on the BDDC method's efficiency, identifying scenarios where the complexity degrades to $O(nz^3)$ due to the solver's impact on the BDDC's convergence. To illustrate the theoretical findings, the research includes numerical experiments for a range of problems, systems, and solver scenarios. Ultimately, the analysis and accompanying numerical examples demonstrate the BDDC's ability to achieve efficient solutions for large linear systems, even when employing inexact solvers within its framework. The research offers the opportunity to further optimize the method's performance through the selection of underlining linear solver parameters. The code utilized in this research is publicly accessible within the PASCAL-SCC project on GitHub. The research also contributes to the ongoing development of the PASCAL-SCC project, aimed at exploring the performance of iterative solvers and preconditioners for linear systems, as demonstrated by the presented BDDC implementation. The project's code is available for public review and is part of the PASCAL-SCC repository on GitHub. We present an updated condition for the existence of a limiting spectral distribution for symmetric matrices with independent entries, whose conditions are more permissive than previous requirements of identical or nearly identical distributions for all entry submatrices. This more flexible condition enables us to establish convergence of the empirical spectral distribution under parameters $\beta_n = n^{\theta-1}$ for any $\theta > 1$ in the case of non-identically distributed entry submatrices. A more stringent condition is necessary to ensure convergence almost surely. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability and precision of these conditions through numerical examples and theoretical guarantees derived from our main findings. These results surpass previous limitations set by the methods of Baik, Devi, and Shyam (2020) and outperform the efficiency of the methods of Bai and Yin (2015) and Wang and Zhou (2014) under more general entry submatrix conditions. We also introduce an efficient and simple estimator for the spectral distribution, along with a method for selecting its key parameters, and provide a guarantee for its correctness under specific conditions. We evaluate the performance of this estimator through simulated numerical examples. All source files associated with the results presented in this study have been made available online at a specified repository.

Quantifying and comparing the masking of gradient information, a phenomenon observed in neural networks when training with adversarial examples, is explored in this study. We propose a metric called GM-score to evaluate the degree of gradient information leakage at different training iterations. Additionally, we conduct various comparisons between conducting training with adversarial examples on traditional neural networks, and investigating our proposals on fresh datasets. The successful creation of acoustic metamaterials at the microscale relies on a thorough understanding of how fluid dynamics influence their macroscopic equivalent behavior. A major limitation in doing so lies in accurately modeling the hydrodynamic interactions of individual fluid molecules at the microscale. Acetic vapor was employed in an acoustics-based toggle switch demonstration, taking advantage of the strong, nonlinear interactions between acetic vapor molecules and the influence of temperature on its viscosity in defining a specific length scale. Through minimization of a dissipation rate function subject to constraints, a nonlinear boundary condition was determined for a surface boundary that models the effects of thermoviscous influences on fluid behavior. Numerical simulations validated the effectiveness of this approach in accurately modeling the behavior of the fluid layer, even in cases where traditional boundary layer theory fails. As a result, this method enabled the reliable prediction of both local and global acoustics in the system, leading to insights that could be applied to various resonant cavities and geometries. Consequently, this approach provides a robust framework for designing acoustic metamaterials that exploit the unique properties of thermoviscous forces and may also inform the development of strategies to manipulate fluid molecule interactions in other contexts. Furthermore, this study showcases a self-sustaining acoustic switch design in action.

Deep neural network classifiers have revolutionized the field of computer science, particularly in image recognition tasks. Despite their remarkable performance, traditional DNNs are prone to a significant drawback: they are unable to provide reliable confidence levels in their predictions. This paper explores a method of constructing a robust uncertainty assessment for a pre-trained DNN classifier using a statistical test on predictive probabilities. This approach, which involves using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare the actual and expected predictive distributions, enables the detection of instances with mismatched predicted and actual probability distributions. By applying this method to a batch of inferences, we can identify and filter out predictions with insufficient confidence, i.e., those with unexpected probability distributions. Our experimental results demonstrate that by incorporating uncertainty assessment using KS-based method, a pre-trained DNN classifier can be modified to provide a level of robustness similar to that achieved through extensive fine-tuning. This technique also enables the detection of predictions with different types of semantic uncertainties, i.e., those with accurate but application-irrelevant classification and those with classification errors due to incomplete or misleading information. Our approach offers a practical solution for addressing uncertainty in deep neural networks, enabling the creation of reliable and confident machine learning systems. Additionally, this technique can be applied to various other machine learning models, revealing its universal applicability. To adapt and robustify reinforcement learning algorithms, they must effectively handle shifts in the problem distribution. While various evaluation tasks have been created to assess this ability, most existing studies lack a central, unified framework for analysis. To address this, we introduce a unifying CURRICULUM-RL benchmark that aggregates multiple task environments representing gradual changes in a learner's curriculum. These environments cover nine categories of change types and assess the ability of reinforcement learning agents to adapt across different transitions, making it possible to compare their adaptability across multiple scenarios. Through the application of a standardized evaluation procedure to multiple benchmark RL scenarios, we gather data on the performance of leading RL algorithms as they navigate this CURRICULUM-RL benchmark. Our study employs this benchmark to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the adaptability of policy optimization, actor-critic, model-free, and model-based RL algorithms. The results indicate that while these algorithms exhibit some ability to adapt in isolation, they often struggle to handle complex curricula. Additionally, we observe that change types influence the relative performance of algorithms in distinct ways. To further investigate the underlying dynamics, we explore the concept of 'activation latency' to describe the extent to which an algorithm must experience a change before its performance improves. We examine the role of this activation latency in relation to change type, algorithm design, and whether an agent is learning online or offline. Our research reveals that activation latency is a critical, yet understudied aspect of the adaptation dynamics in RL. As such, we suggest that future studies prioritize its consideration and seek to develop theories that can capture its influence. All data and code associated with this study have been made available for public access.

Using end mirrors to contain quantum states within an optical setup results in altered imaging properties and a changed relationship between spatial entanglement and Schmidt number. We demonstrate that the Schmidt number no longer serves as a definitive measure of the entanglement's severity, as it is instead influenced by the imaging process. A specific mode of operation, known as the "standard mirror setup," allows us to isolate two-specific entangled modes of operation, and we utilize this setup to investigate the interconnection between spatial entanglement and imaging properties. Furthermore, we propose a simple quantum entanglement test that utilizes a basic setup to assess the entanglement of spatial states produced by any given source. We also examine the behavior of a particular high-Schmidt-number state as it passes through the standard mirror setup, and we find that it exhibits enhanced contrast in the test configuration. This finding prompts us to explore the concept of "high-contrast" states and propose a related definition for high-Schmidt-number states in imaging applications. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of our findings to quantum imaging and suggest possible avenues for further research.

Early warning signs for population collapse have long been a subject of interest, particularly how small variations in conditions can lead to a sudden population shift. A simple and flexible theoretical model incorporates features of weakly coupled, chaotic ecosystems by using a combination of deterministic and stochastic elements. Specifically, this model exhibits point bifurcations, and we identify how the location of these critical points can be predicted using a condition for a non-degenerate bifurcation, even in the presence of noise. This prediction allows us to identify a range of parameters where a stable population exists. Additionally, we analyze a scenario involving the coexistence of two species and find that in this case, a warning period can be predicted before the extinction of one species. This prediction is linked to the geometry of a hypersurface that marks the onset of a coupling advantage for the second species. Finally, we apply this model to analyze a scenario involving the spread of a new species and find that its success can be predicted based on whether it can exploit a previously unoccupied niche. If so, it will spread rapidly. If not, the species will go extinct. This model provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to a wide range of ecosystems, and we demonstrate this with a numerical simulation of a continuous system. This simulation involves the spread of a new species in a circular domain and demonstrates the model's ability to predict the success or failure of the species. This model also highlights the importance of a balance between individual flexibility and the need for a species to adapt to its environment in order to survive and thrive. This balance is achieved when a species is able to occupy a niche that is neither too flexible nor too rigid. This research has significant implications for the ongoing debate over the nature of complex systems and whether they are best described as either fully ordered or fully chaotic. This study demonstrates that many complex systems, including population dynamics, are characterized by a combination of elements from both simple and chaotic systems. Transfer learning has proven highly effective across various NLP tasks, enabling a pre-trained model to be adaptable in languages other than those it was initially trained on. We investigated this capability with BERT, specifically testing its ability to classify sentiments in Vietnamese, a language that significantly differs from English. Our research involved fine-tuning BERT on three sentiment classification datasets in Vietnamese, with one being a large-scale dataset of product reviews. Interestingly, we discovered that BERT exhibited poor performance when used alone but performed satisfactorily when combined with a character-level CNN feature extractor, ultimately achieving a high accuracy rate of 95.6% on the test dataset. Notably, our approach also succeeded in sentiment classification tasks on two other datasets without using any external resources specifically tailored for those datasets, achieving accuracy rates of 86.4% and 79.5% on the Senti-VN dataset and the VASW dataset, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of BERT in NLP tasks outside the English language and provide practical guidance for conducting similar transfer learning tasks in Vietnamese. Additionally, our code and model have been made publicly available to facilitate further research and advancements in sentiment classification and transfer learning in Vietnamese. This research introduces an automated technique for verifying and improving the performance of cache coherence protocols in multiprocessors under sequential consistency. This approach, tailored for protocols utilizing hierarchical caches similar to those found in modern CPUs, automatically checks the correctness of programs and optimizes fence insertions to prevent unnecessary data dependencies, thus speeding up program execution. Specifically, this method inserts caches coherence fences only at program points where data dependenciesoriginating from different processors may lead to a conflict, effectively prioritizing program order over memory order. This tailored fence insertion is determined by a novel dataflow analysis, and has been found to enhance PAMPAS's performance for memory-intensive applications by a factor of up to eight on a dual-core machine, and by up to three on a quad-core machine. Further, this approach's effectiveness is unaffected by the number of cache levels. As an added benefit, fence insertion is now fast enough to be considered a feasible compilation option, and could be an viable strategy for compiler optimizers, even when protocols are not considered. This approach has been validated against state-of-the-art protocol generators, and its performance and correctness have been verified through actual hardware tests, as well as through simulations. This technique's principles can also be applied to other memory consistency models. As an added contribution of this research, a hierarchical fence language called HFL has been designed and implemented, allowing programmers to define custom fence insertion policies that can be executed at cache levels, further enabling the compilation of programs that depend on specific fence insertions for performance. As an example of this language's capabilities, this research demonstrates the compilation of a mail server program that requires specific fence insertions to avoid data conflicts, resulting in an 8 factor performance improvement. This research's findings and HFL's language design make it feasible to compile programs with specific fence insertion requirements, and could lead to better compiler optimization of programs that depend on memory consistency. This research is applicable to any multi-processor system that adheres to sequential consistency and utilizes hierarchical caches. Given a Borel set $A$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we investigate the conditions under which a density function associated with fractional Brownian motion exists and is continuous for $H>1/2$. We examine sets $A$ with varying dimensions to determine the efficacy of an approximation method. Specifically, we establish that when the Hausdorff dimension of $A$ is greater than $d(H)-1$, a continuous density function exists. Conversely, we demonstrate that if the Hausdorff dimension of $A$ is less than $d(H)-1$, this density function is discontinuous, thereby providing an alternative proof of a recent result. We also validate the efficacy of an approximation method when the Hausdorff dimension of $A$ is equal to $d(H)-1$. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the local behavior of the density function near points in $A$.

Early intervention and targeted allocation of resources are crucial in the fight against the COVID-19 pandemic's overwhelming impact on ICU systems.  By analyzing data from hospitalized patients with COVID-19, we can prioritize resource distribution, especially in areas with limited ICU capacity.  We propose a method for predicting ICU requirements among unventilated COVID-19 patients based on easily obtainable clinical features, which can also be applied to identify high-risk patients.  Our approach utilizes a probabilistic neural network to estimate the probability of each patient requiring ICU treatment, as well as the time frame in which they will need it.  By analyzing data from two hospitals in the United States, we found that our model can accurately predict ICU needs with 0.92 AUC, and that certain patient characteristics increase the probability of them needing ICU care.  By targeting these high-risk patients, we can identify 0.25 of patients who will eventually need ICU care 7-10 days later.  This allows for the possible redirection of ICU resources to these patients, which could potentially be done through real-time data analysis in ICU systems. We tackle the challenging task of visual relationship detection, specifically addressing the issue of models converging to a stable state where incorrect relationships are consistently predicted as unknown. This problem arises because the standard classification loss causes the model to favor unlabelled relationships over incorrectly labelled ones. To resolve this issue, we analyze the issues with the standard loss function and propose the Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS) strategy, which involves sampling balanced negative proposals to refine the model. We further integrate this strategy with existing proposal quality evaluation methods, developing a simpler and more effective approach that is robust to parameter changes. By implementing the BNPS strategy, we are able to achieve significant improvements in detection accuracy and model convergence on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results. Moreover, our method achieves comparable performance to the current best result on the LSO VCs dataset without employing large-scale models. Notably, the proposed simple loss function is 150 times faster than the iterative method for least squares optimization. We have open-sourced our code and dataset at https://github.com/whui2016/BNPS.

This study explores the complex nature of action recognition, looking at both unsupervised and supervised learning in this domain. In the context of large, labeled datasets, action recognition is primarily influenced by bounding box placement and labeling errors. Conversely, small, labeled datasets pose a different challenge, where the primary consideration is collecting relevant data. Aspects like data size, quality, and utility are crucial here. This research investigates the impact of training dataset size on error rates in supervised action recognition, revealing that increases in size result in diminishing returns after a certain point. A method called ActionSearch is presented to address this issue by systematically pruning actions from the training set based on their recognition errors, fine-tuning models on the resulting subset until the optimal action is identified. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate that ActionSearch achieves optimal action recognition performance on both large and small datasets, outperforming existing methods. In particular, ActionSearch yields accurate results on small datasets with low lying scores, successfully identifying the target action in as few as 1-5 trials. The formation of galaxies is influenced by the accretion of nearby systems, 
which can result in distinct patterns of star and gas formation. The fate 
of these accretion streams, whether they merge with the primary galaxy or 
become self-sustained, determines the galaxy's structural development. 
Using high-resolution simulations of galaxy formation within a cosmological 
context, this study examines the effect of accretion streams on galaxy growth. 
It finds that such streams typically contain young stars and molecular gas, 
which give them sufficient mass to resist dissolution. As a result, accretion 
streams maintain their identity and contribute to the galaxy's satellite population. 
They contribute to the galaxy's stellar disk through minor mergers, but have a 
limited effect on its central black hole growth. This process results in distinct 
features in the galaxy's global structure and chemical composition patterns. 
However, the galaxy's large-scale structure and velocity dispersion remain unaffected. 
This research highlights the importance of minor mergers in galaxy evolution, 
especially in explaining the observed distributions of satellite galaxies and 
chemical abundance patterns in the Milky Way and similar galaxies. It also 
suggests that galaxy disks with high central black hole masses may have experienced 
minor mergers with massive supermassive black holes. Furthermore, it implies 
that galaxy rotation curves may provide evidence for the presence of accretion 
streams, as they contain extended stellar components that interact with the parent 
galaxy in a manner consistent with minor mergers. This research paves the way 
for exploring the effect of accretion streams on the growth of supermassive black 
holes and the thermal emission from galaxy disks. It also highlights the need 
for high-resolution simulations of galaxy formation, as necessary for studying 
the microcosm of galaxy evolution. Finally, it suggests observing galaxy streams 
in the local universe with surveys of stellar streams and satellite galaxies, 
especially those located at angles of 45 degrees in relation to the major 
axis of the parent galaxy, as predicted by the simulations. This research was 
carried out using the N-body simulations of the MASH-1 simulation, a high-resolution 
simulation of a 100 Mpc/h box, with a focus on the galaxy designated as S0. 
All simulations described in this research were conducted with the GADGET-3 code.

By introducing a complex flavon connected to both neutrino sectors, we maintain the simplicity of the utz setup while solving the stability issue. We then shift from predicting individual neutrino mass values to instead focusing on the utz-derived relationship between these masses, validating that it aligns with observed neutrino oscillation and decay patterns. Consequently, we establish a minimum fundamental scale for this theory, either above the electroweak scale for a specific texture configuration or at the grand unified scale for another, with distinct implications on the utz utl framework. Finally, we outline the potential design of future experiments that could directly or indirectly detect signs of this utz phenomenon, perhaps even revealing the neutrino mass hierarchy through precision beta decay measurements. This could lead to a verification or modification of the utz theory by the mid-21st century. Consequently, this could prompt a reevaluation of the neutrino mass scale, potentially necessitating a revision of the utl parameter space, with implications for dark matter direct detection experiments operating at or below the scale of the neutrino mass hierarchy. Ultimately, a utz-driven shift in the understanding of neutrino properties will have far-reaching consequences for dark matter research and multiscalar dark matter models. By leveraging a static program analyzer that provides weakly supervised training data,
we propose a method to enhance neural program generators using a counterexample-guided
training approach. Our approach starts with a basic neural network that is trained
on the analyzer's output and can already produce programs from examples. Through
counterexample analysis, we identify programs that differ from desired outcomes
and associate them with specific error messages from the analyzer. By refining
the network with these programs and error messages, we improve program accuracy.
Our experiments show that this approach successfully enhances neural program
generators in multiple settings and outperforms alternative methods for
correcting program errors. The trained models and source code for our study
are available online.

We introduce an incremental anomaly detection technique for high-dimensional data, which builds upon the capabilities of one-class neural networks. By refining the previous model's parameters and adding new data, the proposed method allows for real-time anomaly detection with minimal training time. Unlike conventional approaches that require collecting comprehensive anomaly-free data from scratch, this method can effectively handle data collected over time with only limited annotation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing its results to a method that trains the network from scratch for each new dataset component, which is impractically slow for large datasets. We evaluate the proposed method on both synthetic and real-world data, showing that it achieves comparable accuracy to the baseline method that has access to the entire dataset at once. However, the proposed method is significantly faster, particularly for large datasets. We also explore the impact of different activation functions and layer architectures on the network's performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/krzysztof-czarnacki/IncAnomOAA. The paper has been accepted for publication in the journal Neural Networks.

A seemingly innocuous property of an encryption scheme, denyability, implies a
pernicious consequence: in certain situations, the government can compel decryption
without a court order. We analyze key constructions of public-key and private-key
encryption with this property and find that even when the encryption is secure
against a computationally bounded adversary, it can be forced open by an
adversary with sufficient computational power. We examine specific constructions
of public-key and private-key encryption that achieve this property and explore
its implications for encryption in general. We propose a framework for safe denial
symmetric encryption and a construction of public-key encryption with certain
deniable properties, along with an analysis of its security. We also consider
the interplay between encryption and randomness generation and present an
adversarial attack on a particular type of encryption. We based our research on prior works by Helly-Henry, Naor and Ostrovsky, and Waidner and Hartmann. We believe our findings have implications for the safety of data encryption methods.
