Building meaningful sentence representations from generative neural networks is challenging, especially when these networks are trained to capture a large vocabulary. To circumvent this issue, we developed SparseGAN, a pioneering technique that incorporates a sparse activation pattern in the hidden layers of a generative network while optimizing the activation probabilities with a sentence representation constraint. This activation probability optimization process is achieved through adversarial training with a density estimator, allowing us to obtain a compact and semantic sentence representation from the learned sparse code. Through multiple evaluations, SparseGAN exhibited not only enhanced paragraph-level semantic representation but also improved sentence representations when combined with generative models, leading to better performance in downstream tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis. Our findings also revealed that SparseGAN can produce more semantically coherent sentences than comparable methods from the natural language generation community. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/hahnfeng/SparseGAN.

Open star clusters in late stages of evolution are often sought after in the search for evidence of interstellar panspermia, specifically for microbial life that could have originated from another planetary system. To assess the viability of panspermia in these clusters, a statistical analysis is required of the temporal relationships between the stars' birth events, including star formations, deaths, and potential planetary material transmissions. Using observations and theoretical stellar evolution models, I calculated the time scales for the generation and dissemination of planetary material in multiple late-stage open star clusters. The results show that the dispersal of microbial life between stars could have occurred in three of these clusters, specifically NGC 6704, NGC 6773, and Berkeley 76. Notably, NGC 6704 exhibits a significant time span of roughly 10 million years between the birth of its longest-lived star and the death of a hotter companion, indicating a possible panspermia event. However, to confirm this finding, more data are needed to constrain the cluster's age and stellar parameters. Additionally, a search for extraterrestrial life should prioritize regions surrounding cool red giant stars, as these stars offer the most favorable conditions for interstellar panspermia. Lastly, I propose that future observations of late-stage open star clusters should be accompanied by targeted searches for astronomical biosignatures, including the detection of oxygen, carbon, and water vapor, as well as remote monitoring of stellar activity, which could indicate the presence of microbial life influencing the star's behavior. Ultimately, a comprehensive analysis of these clusters will allow for a more accurate assessment of the possibility of interstellar panspermia. To this end, I suggest establishing a multidisciplinary team to explore the intersection of astrobiology, astronomy, and physics within the context of these star clusters. By doing so, we may uncover compelling evidence for the existence of interstellar life.

This work proposes a novel, three-tiered model of dark matter, which posits that dark matter consists of three distinct components, each associated with a specific cosmic era: the present day, the early universe, and the cosmological intermediate period. During the present day, dark matter is composed of solitons and vortices in a $SU(3)$ symmetry-breaking scenario, which influences the behavior of dark matter particles like dark photons and millicharged particles. In the early universe, dark matter took the form of axions, which were generated by the decay of dark mesons produced during the universe's hadronization phase. Finally, in the cosmologically intermediate period, dark matter existed as dark mesons, which were strongly interacting particles that essentially made up a dark version of the quark gluon plasma. This model predicts that dark matter could be directly detected only in the present day, while in earlier eras, dark matter's presence would be indicated by signatures of axion production and dark meson decay, respectively. Notably, the masses of dark matter particles across the three tiers are intertwined by cosmological constraints and theoretical considerations. This three-tiered framework also provides an alternative explanation for the matter-antimatter asymmetry and the cosmological dark matter density in comparison to existing theories. Finally, this model offers testable predictions regarding direct, indirect, and collider dark matter detection, as well as implications for big-bang nucleosynthesis, axion astronomy, and the effective number of neutrino species. This could potentially allow us to differentiate between this three-tiered model and other dark matter theories through multi-faceted means. This work can serve as a starting point for a more in-depth exploration of a dark matter physics framework that integrates both direct and indirect detection, as well as cosmological aspects. This could potentially allow us to integrate other effective field theories of dark matter, such as the one proposed in [2], where dark matter is composed of solitons and vortices, with the rest of the dark matter spectrum being described by a effective field theory. This three-tiered model of dark matter offers a coherent and self-consistent picture of the universe's dark matter composition across all eras, from the present day back to the early universe. Animal population studies are a fundamental component of ecological and biological research, and a growing number of studies are using camera traps. A recently developed method from statistical genetics called spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models has shown potential for accurate population density estimates. However, the application of SCR to camera trap data has limitations due to the high computational demand of its underlying Bayesian model. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a random forest (RF) predictor that uses camera trap data to estimate population density according to the SCR model. Our RF approach includes multiple features that are typically excluded from SCR models, such as animal age and sex, which are often difficult to obtain. By incorporating these additional features, we are able to estimate capture probability at a specific location, and our results show that these estimates correlate strongly with actual capture data. Our method also allows us to map capture probability spatially, which can inform research design and guide data collection in future studies. We demonstrate the practical applications of our RF approach using camera trap data from a real-world animal population study. Our results suggest that RF can provide accurate population density estimates and capture probability maps that are comparable to SCR models. Notably, our approach yields these estimates with significantly less computational demand. We also provide a user-friendly R package called rcams that enables users to apply our RF approach to their own camera trap data. This package includes a graphical user interface and enables users to access the underlying data through a Shiny application. We believe that our RF approach and associated R package will be a valuable tool for researchers and conservationists working with camera trap data. We also anticipate that our approach can be adapted for use in other capture-recapture studies that employ automated counters. In graph theory, particularly in the study of network connectivity, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem is a critical component. This problem involves identifying the k edge disjoint paths between nodes s and t in a graph while minimizing the total energy expenditure. This problem has practical applications in various fields, including healthcare and multi-path routing protocols. However, solving this problem analytically is extremely challenging due to the complex relationships between power levels and graph connectivity. In an attempt to address this limitation, a simulation-based approach known as Simulation-Based Optimization (SBO) is proposed, leveraging the capabilities of SCPy to integrate multiple simulation tools and optimize graph connectivity through energy minimization. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, a series of simulations were conducted using both a simple Python script and more complex scenarios, including an instance with up to 16 nodes. The results showed that the SBO method can effectively determine the minimum power required to create k edge disjoint paths in a graph, even in complex scenarios, demonstrating its potential as a robust solution for solving Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problems. Furthermore, this approach may be applied to address other graph connectivity challenges. A Python implementation of the SCPy solver is also included as a means to facilitate further research and collaboration. A companion technical report provides additional methodological details and results for all conducted simulations. A network connectivity application case study, involving the optimization of wireless sensor network configurations to detect specific communication patterns, is also presented. This study is particularly relevant to the healthcare industry, specifically in the context of medical device connectivity and reconfigurable sensor networks. In this research, we apply the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) filter to a swarm of 50 vehicles, simulating real-world scenarios with multiple sensors, and investigate how to prioritize target management based on their likelihood and location. However, our findings also indicate that the best approach can be sensor-dependent, and a more flexible algorithm that adapts to changing target situations is required for optimal performance. This transition is key to understanding how information and diseases spread in complex networks, particularly those with broad distribution scales. Near the transition point, a substantial decentralized component emerges, affecting the spread of the epidemic. Interestingly, this decentralized component is controlled by the same critical exponent as the size of the largest centralized component, indicating a relationship between them. This finding is notable, as it implies that targeting the decentralized component near the transition point can yield valuable information about the network's structure and size. Additionally, this discovery enables the development of more effective strategies to control the spread of the epidemic. Through numerical simulations, it has been shown that targeting the decentralized component can significantly reduce the epidemic prevalence, even if the epidemic has already been spread widely. We introduce Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), an innovative approach that enhances conventional Recurrent State Space Models through a separate recurrent process for latent variables and observations. This structure enables the learning and inference of complex, partially dynamic systems from multiple, correlated data sources. We demonstrate that HiP-RSSMs can be trained using the Expectation Maximization algorithm and derive a computational efficient learning method based on the Alternating Least Squares technique. Furthermore, we establish that HiP-RSSMs can be viewed as a specific instance of the Multivariate Pitman-Yor Process, allowing us to apply the Dynamic Texture Inference framework. This results in a method for inferring hidden system dynamics and allocating data between sources. We evaluate HiP-RSSMs on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it outperforms traditional RSSMs on learning and inference tasks. Additionally, HiP-RSSMs can effectively divide complex data into segments that correspond to distinct system dynamics. This is highlighted by the model's performance on the dataset consisting of movements of a fish expressed by disturbing the water. HiP-RSSMs also facilitate the study of complex systems with multiple, dynamic processes by automatically identifying the allocation of data among sources. This is demonstrated through the modeling of a system featuring two interacting, but distinct, subsystems. We also explore HiP-RSSMs in a setting with no prior knowledge about the system's dynamics, leading to the discovery of hidden system variables through the inference process. This is showcased on a dataset depicting the movement of a fish with an externally imposed dynamic. HiP-RSSMs can be trained on GitHub, and the code for this work is hosted on this repository. Measuring the degree of polarization in social networks is crucial for analyzing cluster formation, but the variety of methods employed for this purpose demands a closer examination. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of methods used to measure polarization from 2005 to 2020 by conducting a systematic review. We evaluated and critically assessed 33 different measures used in 72 studies, identifying key factors that influence the results, including method application, data type, and data source. The methods were categorized into four types: induced, prescriptive, descriptive, and additional methods. We developed a conceptual framework explaining the application of methods based on their induced vs. prescriptive and descriptive vs. additional characteristics. We also created a taxonomy of methods used in polarization measurement, associated with a corresponding R package. This taxonomic system can be utilized for calculating the methods, and we incorporated an assessment tool that indicates the applicability of each method to a given network structure. This tool can be accessed through the PolMeasures package available on CRAN. We further explored the relationship between methods, considering structural and relational aspects, and proposed a novel, integrated measure that combines elements from polarization measures. This study's findings can inform researchers on the best methods to use for measuring polarization in social networks, and the PolMeasures package provides researchers with a convenient tool for calculating the methods and assessing their applicability. However, measuring polarization is a complex task, and there is no single "right" method. Therefore, it is essential to thoroughly evaluate and justify the methods employed for this purpose. This study's goals are to provide a comprehensive critique of methods used for measuring polarization in social networks and to offer practical guidance for researchers on the best methods to use, available as an R package for easy calculation and assessment. This is particularly relevant for research in politics, sociology, and economics. In politics, measures of polarization are crucial for analyzing cluster formation and voting patterns. In sociology, polarization analysis is used for studying friendship and community formations. In economics, measures of polarization are employed for analyzing income and wealth distributions. Despite its significance, a comprehensive critique of methods used for measuring polarization is lacking. This study aims to address this gap by providing a systematic review of methods employed for this purpose. This is particularly relevant for research in politics, sociology, economics, and other fields where social networks are studied. Recent studies have demonstrated that adding promotions or utilizing promt engineering techniques can facilitate NLP tasks by leveraging a small amount of task data. However, existing methods face obstacles in scaling to various tasks and fine-tuning NLP models due to the need for task-specific data and adjustments to the model's parameter configuration. In this research, we introduce HyperPrompt, a groundbreaking NLP model that incorporates HyperNetworks to efficiently handle multiple NLP tasks by utilizing a small amount of task data. By establishing connections between prompt engineering and hypernetworks, we successfully transformed prompt-based task labels into hypernetworks that can be applied to NLP models with minimal additional computational expense. Our experiments indicate that HyperPrompt achieves notable improvements over baseline models in NLP tasks, resulting in precise performance on low-shot tasks and notable boosts in performance on more demanding tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt was found to surpass the performance of state-of-the-art parametric prompt tuning methods in low-shot settings and match the performance of non-HyperNetwork-based high-shot shot-free baselines. Moreover, our analysis suggests that HyperPrompt excels in processing natural language inputs by effectively exploiting the structural characteristics of language and overcoming the limitations of sequence-to-sequence transformations. Our study indicates that HyperPrompt's capability to leverage task data allows NLP models to adapt to new tasks with ease, paving the way for more flexible and versatile pre-trained NLP models. In this paper, we examine the root systems of types A_l and D_l, focusing on the longest root and its connection to other roots within the system. This analysis enables us to establish upper limits for the number of roots at various distances from the longest root. Additionally, we can determine the number of roots that lie on a specific hyperplane defined by a given root. This insight can be applied to set bounds on the number of roots within a particular angle or sector centered on the longest root. Furthermore, we derive a minimum value for the product of the coordinates of the longest root, providing a quantitative measure of the longest root's direction. This direction is significant as it is orthogonal to the direction of the highest weight of the irreducible root system in types A_l and B_l. We also explore the concept of a'most distant' root, which may not be unique, and may be distinct from the longest root. In the case of root systems of type A_l, we find that the most distant root can be expressed as a sum of the longest root and a root from a reduced root system of type A_(l-1). Similarly, in the case of root systems of type D_l, we can express the most distant root as the sum of the longest root and a root from a reduced root system of type D_(l-1), specifically containing the most distant root from that subsystem. Lastly, we can determine the number of positive roots within the root system, and can further refine this count by considering only the roots that lie on a specific hyperplane defined by a given root. We introduce a novel randomized distributed algorithm for estimating the size of a connected static network that takes the form of a tree. The network is inhabited by nodes that have unique identifiers and can execute independent calculations, and these calculations are used to determine the network's size. The algorithm is designed to run in $O(\log k)$ rounds and $O(\log k/\epsilon^2)$ time units, where $k$ represents the network size, and it is trained to return an estimate $\hat{n}$ that satisfies the condition $|n-\hat{n)|\leq n/\epsilon$ with a probability of at least $1-\epsilon$. The proposed approach is the first to achieve this level of accuracy in a tree-based network via a fully distributed approach, and it improves upon the existing worst-case bounds in both time and round complexity. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through both theoretical and practical means, and it has been found to perform well in various types of networks, including those with power law properties, through means of both simulation and real-world application. This conclusion is based on a comparison of mean absolute percentages errors (MAPE) for both nonparametric and parametric methods under varying conditions of service rate, arrival rate, and simulation duration. Our data shows that nonparametric estimation yields more reliable results across all scenarios even when the underlying assumptions of the parametric method are met. Additionally, our research reveals that the accuracy of both methods is ultimately determined by the relative rates of arrival and service, and that neither is significantly influenced by the exponential distribution's characteristic time until the first customer or the time until a specific number of customers are present. Our findings are relevant to any M/M/1 queue with arrival rates greater than the service rate, where the queue is not empty and has a specific number of customers. Our study's results are applicable to systems that experience low to moderate traffic, and it is suggested that a notional queue of 100 customers be used as a standard for comparison in future similar studies. Global electromagnetic fluctuations, significant at the edge of a tokamak, have a major influence on the transport of particles and heat. Globally active modes (GAMs), observed in several devices, are likely affected by these fluctuations and may play a key role in the development of turbulent transport. This study focuses on GAMs in the edge plasma of the Tore-Supra tokamak and reveals that the growth rates of these modes are directly proportional to the square root of the electron-to-ion temperature ratio, inversely proportional to the square of the electron gyro-radius, and insensitive to the magnetic flux surface area. Additionally, GAMs are found to be quasi-modes, with low frequency compared to the ion cyclotron frequency, and are stabilized by the ion motion. A comparison between fluid and kinetic theories shows good agreement, with the ratio of GAM growth rates also matching the expected values from kinetic theory. The results also indicate that increasing the electron temperature will lead to a rise in GAM growth rates, which could contribute to the enhancement of turbulent transport in the tokamak edge. This study provides further evidence that GAMs share a common origin with flow gaps and grain modes, and that the ion circulation angle induced by these modes could be a key factor in determining the electron heat flux. Consequently, GAMs may play a significant role in the development of turbulent electron heat transport. Further experimental and theoretical study is required to fully understand the impact of GAMs on plasma confinement. Quantum annealing is an optimization technique that relies on gradual changes to be applied to constrained problems. However, environment interference may hinder its effectiveness, causing the loss of a desired ground state. We examine environments that induce coherent and incoherent processes and find that decoherence can both enhance and impede the success of quantum annealing, depending on the duration of the process. Additionally, we find that environmental coherent processes can result in the loss of a target ground state due to quantum interference, and that this phenomenon is observable in both spin glass and constrained satisfaction problems. Furthermore, we investigate the potential improvement of quantum annealing through interactions with a coherent environment, and find that this may not always yield beneficial results. Finally, we propose a new quantum annealing schedule that incorporates environmental influences to improve its chances of success. This schedule exhibits the ability to overcome obstacles that conventional methods struggle with. Through the use of a spin glass model, we demonstrate the capability of this environment-informed quantum annealing to outperform conventional methods across a range of environmental conditions. Additionally, we find that this approach has the potential to enhance performance in constrained satisfaction and random k-satisfiability problems. However, its potential to outperform conventional methods in actual applications awaits further exploration. Despite significant progress in recent years, deep neural networks still require large amounts of labeled data to achieve high levels of accuracy. This limitation stems from the extensive parameters of these networks, which results in them failing to effectively learn from limited, sparse labeled data. One potential solution to this challenge is to use local trained networks for dense, unsupervised or supervised learning, as this could allow for the efficient use of labeled data. In this study, we examine two types of neural networks: convolutional and recurrent – and demonstrate that learning at a local level can be both efficient and accurate. We propose a novel LCT (Local Critic Training) method which involves training local networks on the entire available dataset without segmentation. This allows for the generation of highly accurate and dense labels on the entire dataset for a fraction of the cost of traditional supervised learning. We apply LCT to two types of networks: A CNN and an RNN, and achieve notable improvements in learning density and accuracy. Our findings indicate that learning at a local level can be both efficient and accurate, and that LCT is an effective and practical solution for deep neural networks to handle sparse labeled data. Additionally, LCT is a general method that can be used for supervised and semi-supervised learning. It is also compatible with other pre-training methods such as contrastive learning. We anticipate that LCT will be of interest to researchers working in deep neural networks, and encourage them to explore its application in other network architectures. We have made our code and data available for public access.

We present a modified version of the Lotka-Volterra model that incorporates active predator-prey interactions, where the reaction rates for predation and the increase in prey populations depend on the respective intelligence parameters. By applying mean field theory, we analyze the model's equilibrium solutions and phase portraits to explore how different levels of intelligence influence the coexistence of species. Notably, this model replicates the phenomenon of swarms exhibiting different levels of complexity, as seen in actual insect swarms. Numerical simulations are used to compare the outcomes of this model with actual recorded data. In conclusion, this model demonstrates that active predator-prey interactions, in conjunction with distinct intelligence levels, can induce intricate dynamics leading to the extinction or coexistence of species, even in the absence of random fluctuations. Furthermore, we delve into possible justifications for the inclusion of active terms in equations of state, along with potential applications of this model to other systems featuring interacting species. Lastly, we discuss potential research paths for expanding this model, including incorporating spatial dimensions, adaptive intelligence dynamics, and the integration of additional active terms. This model can be an invaluable tool in exploring the dynamic interactions between predator and prey species, as well as providing valuable insights into the effects of different levels of intelligence on ecosystem dynamics. This research can be further utilized to contribute to ongoing discussions in the fields of active fluids, starved ecosystems, and adaptive systems. This model is now available online at the PhysiCell website, along with a companion tutorial that includes code, along with all necessary parameters and files, enabling other researchers to execute the model and explore its capabilities for themselves. This model and tutorial have the potential to advance our understanding of active predator-prey interactions and their effects on ecosystem dynamics, as well as to serve as a valuable educational resource for demonstrating complex dynamical systems in action. Despite notable breakthroughs in learning-based control through imitation, a significant issue remains: the reliance on extensive expert data. This limitation can be particularly challenging to mitigate in complex systems, where obtaining expert knowledge is difficult and costly. In this research, we introduce a novel algorithm that enables controlled learning from just a single demonstration on a physical robot. We frame this problem as policy refinement, starting from a coarse policy that meets basic safety requirements and aim to find a fine-tuned policy minimizing data usage. The proposed method, SISO, utilizes a combination of imitation learning and robust optimization to handle data noise and limited samples, yielding a robust policy that excels in multiple trials. The benefits of SISO are highlighted through experiments on a robotic system, involving the generation of over 2000 episodes from a single expert demonstration, a significant reduction compared to traditional approaches. The results show that SISO successfully discovers a policy 5-7 times more efficient in terms of demonstration count. The findings are further validated by comparing the performance of the learned policies against a baseline method using multiple trials, yielding a 15-20% improvement in efficiency. The methodology is also analyzed in terms of the optimal hyperparameter settings and the implications of noise robust optimization on the results. The work presented has the potential to accelerate the development of controlled learning-based systems by allowing them to work effectively from limited expert data. We introduce a novel method for deriving and demonstrating certain integral and differential identities by leveraging geometric vector-based proofs. This approach, which combines the use of diagrams, geometric proofs, and basic algebra, offers a straightforward and efficient way to establish formulas previously obtained through lengthy computational methods. We illustrate this method by demonstrating a specific identity related to the Gaussian function and its applications. This method can be particularly beneficial for teachers and instructors who wish to present alternative proofs of such identities for students in introductory calculus courses. As an added benefit, this approach also provides a glimpse into more advanced topics in Lie algebra, differential geometry, and representation theory. We also consider a few additional problems that can be solved using this method and suggest a few related research questions for further exploration. One such question concerns the derivation of identities related to Bessel functions, which could potentially be addressed through the application of this method. Finally, we propose that this approach be used to deliver a unique and engaging calculus curriculum that emphasizes problem-solving, visual learning, and the connection between mathematical formulas and their underlying geometric structures. This curriculum could not only help students master fundamental calculus concepts but also equip them with the skills and mindset necessary for tackling more complex challenges in mathematics and physics. As an example, we outline a specific course outline and provide a set of accompanying lecture notes that demonstrate this approach in action. This approach has already been successfully tested with a group of high school students who, as a result of this curriculum, were able to solve various problems, including one related to Kirchhoff's rule, which they had not been previously taught. This experience suggests that this approach not only facilitates the derivation of mathematical formulas but also fosters a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and geometry. As such, it has significant implications for the reform of calculus education and could serve as a model for the development of more effective and engaging curricula in other areas of mathematics and science. This approach can also be adapted for use with different types of functions and identities and could be applied to other areas of mathematics and physics that involve functional identities, such as harmonic analysis, representation theory, and number theory. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to transform the way calculus is taught and learned by making it more visual, intuitive, and connected to the underlying geometry and physics. As such, it could help to address some of the key challenges facing the reform of calculus education, such as the lack of engagement among some students and the failure of many students to develop a deeper understanding of the subject. The anomalous magnetic moment of the muon remains a key area of focus in high-energy physics, where a notable discrepancy exists between theoretical predictions and experimental findings. To further explore this phenomenon, a new experiment has been proposed, known as MuSun, which will be implemented at the J-PET facility in Pakistan and is slated to run from 2024 to 2028, utilizing a 10 times more intense muon beam than the existing MUON program. As a result, MuSun will deliver roughly 30 times more data, which in turn will enable the experiment to investigate the muon scattering data in addition to the magnetic moment. Combining the data from MuSun and the existing MUON program will permit a measurement accuracy of 0.4 parts per billion for the magnetic moment, which is sufficient to address the muon anomaly question. Furthermore, by examining the circular polarization of emitted gamma rays in response to muon scattering from bismuth, which contains the highest possible fraction of the muon's magnetic moment, MuSun can achieve a 10 times improvement in the measurement of the magnetic moment. Ultimately, this will allow MuSun to investigate the parity-violating asymmetry associated with the weak interaction, which was previously measured with accuracy limited by the muon beamline at Brookhaven National Laboratory. As such, MuSun has the capability to explore new physics explanations for the muon anomaly, including several scenarios involving scalar and vector fields that interact with the Higgs boson through various portals. Additionally, by delivering significantly more data than the existing MUON program, which is anticipated to be the primary limitation, a future precision experiment such as MuSun will be poised to take advantage of future theoretical developments in lattice QCD. As a result, MuSun has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to our understanding of the strong and electroweak interactions and may provide valuable insights that could inform future high-energy physics research at the LHC or its potential successors. Finally, it is proposed that MuSun will be implemented at the J-PET facility in Pakistan, which offers a unique combination of scientific and strategic benefits, including the ability to leverage expertise and resources from across the Middle East and South Asia in pursuit of cutting-edge research in high-energy physics. This pilot study compared the remote learning experiences of under-represented minority and non-under-represented minority students in one algebra-based physics class at a large public university in the southeastern United States. Both groups showed similar interest in learning and a tendency to disengage from remote learning, as measured by online module participation. However, under-represented minority students displayed lower levels of online module engagement than their non-under-represented peers, with a larger gap observed in interactive modules. Potential contributing factors to these findings are explored, alongside implications for adapting remote learning strategies to meet the diverse needs of all students. Furthermore, suggestions are made for refining future investigations in this area.

We introduce an axiom called anti-classicality, which postulates the non-existence of non-classical subsets in set theory. Building upon this, we derive the consequence that all non-empty sets contain classical elements. We then investigate various combinations of the anti-classicality axiom with other principles from intuitionistic and classical mathematics. Notably, we show that combining the anti-classicality axiom with countable choice yields a theory that is computationally equivalent to classical ZFC. Conversely, we demonstrate that in the context of full choice, the anti-classicality axiom results in a theory that is strictly weaker than classical ZFC. Lastly, we consider the intersection of the anti-classicality axiom with Kleene intuitionistic arithmetic and examine the resulting theories' relationship to intuitionistic ZF and BZFC. Ultimately, our findings broaden our understanding of the relationships between classical and non-classical elements in set theory and explore the interplay between intuitive and classical set theoretic concepts. These investigations also prompt questions about the applicability of anti-classical elements in constructive mathematics. Lastly, we outline potential directions for future research in this area. These investigations we carry out are set against the backdrop of recent studies on non-classical elements within set theory.

Computing the entropy of a probability distribution is a fundamental task, but this task becomes increasingly difficult when the distribution cannot be directly expressed. This research addresses this challenge by developing an efficient method to calculate the Shannon, Kullback-Liebler, and Hellinger distances for approximate probability distributions, even when these distributions are implied by a data set of symbolic expressions. By applying a recently introduced algorithm for solving linear systems represented by symbolic expressions, this study first presents an innovative approach to compute the entropy of such implied probability distributions. This new algorithmic framework also enables solving linear system representations in the context of maximum-entropy methods for approximating unobservable probability distributions. Consequently, this research provides a groundbreaking solution for computational problems that involve entropy-based objectives with data inputs that are expressed symbolically. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method through a concrete application to a well-known challenge in music information retrieval. Lastly, this research is showcased through a comprehensive implementation using the Emdros information-theoretic inference engine and is accompanied by an open-source code for the described algorithmic framework. This code is now freely available online. Additionally, this study also introduces the use of formally defined functions to enhance the expressiveness of linear system representations and presents an innovative way to utilize ordered algebras in computational entropy calculations. Lastly, this research is expected to contribute positively to the widening stakeholder engagement between the fields of information theory and computational logic. Dynamic graph classifications are significantly more complex to represent than static graphs, due to their ever-changing nature, which demands a more sophisticated representation of structural information. The Deep Neural Network (DNN) typically employs GNNs as building blocks but struggles with temporal dependencies, leading to the proposal of DECENNT, an innovative GWN that incorporates temporal information. DECENNT is distinguished by two key components: Dynamic Neighborhood Network (DNN) and Time-Aggregated Neighborhood Network (TANN). The DNN module utilizes a GNN to identify the current node's feature representation based on neighboring nodes, while the TANN module uses a temporal attention mechanism to combine feature representations from different time points. DECENNT's unique ability to handle temporal information and graph structure enables it to achieve state-of-the-art performance on two classification tasks involving dynamic graphs. The evaluation of DECENNT's components through an ablation study confirms that both DNN and TANN are crucial components with DNN responsible for the graph structure and TANN responsible for temporal information. The comparison of DECENNT with multiple baseline methods supports its superior performance, while the comparison of DECENNT with a similar model without temporal information reveals a significant performance gap. The comparison with models using different pooling mechanisms indicates that DECENNT outperforms them by a considerable margin. The thorough analysis of DECENNT's components and evaluation of its effectiveness make a compelling case for the use of DECENNT in classification tasks involving dynamic graphs. Recent advancements in next-generation sequencing and the decreasing cost of genomic data have made it possible to study population dynamics and reconstruct phylogenetic trees using whole-genome data. As a result, researchers now have access to stochastic processes that enable evolutionary analysis and phylogeny reconstruction. However, before these processes can be utilized, it is essential to estimate the population size and the number of generations that have passed since a particular variant originated. Both of these parameters are critical for understanding evolutionary history and reconstructing phylogenetic trees accurately. In this paper, we introduce three separate Bayesian statistical models to estimate the effective population size, the generation time, and the ancestral coverage of whole-genome variants. We also propose a Bayesian statistical model that enables the reconstruction of phylogenetic trees from quartet trees. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of our estimators on simulated data and apply them to real-world datasets consisting of SARS-CoV-2 genomic data. All of our methods have been implemented in the form of a Python package called EVOQUATE, which is freely accessible for use. This package can be found under the following address: https://github.com/StatFQ/EVOQUATE. The study of temporal cell and molecular patterns is referred to as temporalomics.  Advances in single-cell RNA profiling and protein detection using spatially resolved quantitative mass spectrometry have enhanced the investigation of temporalomics.  Although software for analyzing temporalomics focuses on individual applications, there is a lack of suites that can automatically identify patterns from genetic data, interpret their functional roles, and predict associated disease outcomes.  To address this limitation, we present a comprehensive analysis suite called TempoSuites, incorporating multiple R tools and interface options via Shiny for visualizing and predicting pattern functional roles and clinical implications.  TempoSuites distinguishes itself through its composable analysis approach, allowing for a range of starting points, from identifying patterns from genetic data to predicting clinical implications from those patterns.  The software includes specific R packages like TempoPatterns, TempoRoles, and TempoClinic, and is available under an open-source license on GitHub.  To facilitate easy use, TempoSuites provides step-by-step documentation, along with video tutorials and a community forum on GitHub.  By leveraging this suite, researchers and clinicians can accelerate the analysis of temporalomics data and facilitate a deeper understanding of biological processes at the cellular level.  As such, TempoSuites has the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of temporalomics and, ultimately, the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.  In addition, the software can help automate the comparison of cell and molecular patterns across various species, further enriching its applications in the scientific community.  Ultimately, TempoSuites will provide powerful capabilities for analyzing temporalomics data and its practical uses will be showcased through its integration with publicly available datasets.  In conjunction with this, we will present newly identified patterns discovered through this suite. For a complex optical system, where wave dynamics are highly nontrivial, we make explicit connections between the principles of SU(1,1) representation, intensity distributions, and eigenchannels. We demonstrate that the intensity distributions within the system are derived from the projections of eigenchannels onto specific basis sets, and these sets exhibit the property of orthogonalization at both input and output planes. A numerical example involving a diverging Gaussian beam passing through a microresonator is utilized to visualize and quantify the relationships between the different components, including the intensity distributions, eigenchannels, and their corresponding orthogonal sets. Notably, the degree of orthogonalization is shown to be limited by the amount of phase squeezing in the system, and this has significant implications for the achievement of high-quality mode demultiplication. Our approach offers a straightforward path for the computational investigation of complex wave dynamics in any optical system, and has the added benefit of clarifying the fundamental role of SU(1,1) representation in the analysis of wave phenomena. Additionally, this framework promotes a deeper understanding of the principles underlying mode demultiplication, and could potentially inform the design of optical systems that leverage non-Gaussian beams.

We examine a scenario in which a strong and random potential is applied to a two-dimensional, interacting Luttinger liquid at its transition to a phase of strong correlation. We calculate the disorder-induced topological characteristics of this state and demonstrate how they could be measured in actual experiments. The results show that the topological characters of Anderson insulators can be determined through measurements of the full distribution of local values in a sample, opposed to relying solely on the mean values of these characteristics in specific geometries. Additionally, we find that interacting Luttinger liquids have a tendency towards "frustration-driven topological order", in which interacting Luttinger liquids may exhibit non-trivial topology without the protection of symmetry. This occurs even in instances where the mean values of relevant parameters do not cross any critical thresholds. We anticipate this study to have implications for understanding topological characteristics in disorder systems, multi-component systems, and systems near transitions between different phases. It is also expected to stimulate the development of experimental techniques for detecting the full distribution of local values in physical systems. As an example, we outline a proposal for detecting the topological characters of Anderson insulators in a setup involving transport measurements through a point contact. The paper describes the computational approach taken with L-functions, focusing on a method using Dessin d'Enfants and Mumford's formula for computing invariants directly. A key finding reported indicates that separate computational methods for the same genus-one curves yield identical geometric properties in a significant majority of cases, as determined by the topological and geometric characteristics of the curves' Jacobians. This result supports the independent nature of these geometric properties, which should remain unchanged regardless of the computation method used. The study also establishes a connection between curves computed analytically and their computed invariants, which enables the identification of specific curves with desired geometric properties and sufficient height up to $240$. We explored the production of top quark pairs in association with heavy Higgs bosons at the Large Hadron Collider using next-to-leading order perturbative calculations and leading virtual corrections from the soft collinear subtraction scheme, considering the impact of the CKKW matching procedure on the cross-section results. Our analysis focused specifically on the influence of the CKKW matching radius on the cross-section for squark-induced heavy Higgs boson production, revealing that the radius has a significant effect due to the interference between the squark and gluon contributions. We found that the CKKW matching affects the cross-section more than the underlying soft collinear subtraction scheme, with the influence dependent on the phase of the complex squark mass parameter and the mass of the heavy Higgs boson. On the other hand, we found that the CKKW matching has a minimal impact on the cross-section for the case where the squark contribution is negligible. Additionally, we compared our calculated results to those obtained using the MADGRAPH5\_aMC@NLO generator for both the case with and without the CKKW matching procedure, finding that the CKKW matching has a significant effect on the squark-induced cross-section only when the squark contribution is significant. Notably, we observed that the CKKW matching has a minimal impact on the cross-section when the squark contribution is negligible, with the soft collinear subtraction scheme having an even less noticeable effect in this scenario. Our research is relevant to ongoing and future searches for heavy Higgs bosons at the Large Hadron Collider.

This paper introduces a new statistical test to determine whether a specific network autoregressive model parameter, say $\theta_0$, is identifiable or not.  Due to the complex nature of network autoregressive models, where non-identifiable parameters are a common issue, we focus on evaluating the asymptotic behavior of a test in situations where the true parameter is non-identifiable.  To this end, we propose using the likelihood ratio test, which we show can be effectively modified to tackle non-identifiable parameters.  In particular, we demonstrate that by using the modified test based on the score equation, we can obtain consistent test results, which can be used to determine the asymptotic distribution of the test statistic.  We also establish that the proposed test is sensitive to changes in the true network autoregressive model, which can be used to evaluate the power of the test.  To illustrate the application of the proposed test, we conduct simulations and real-world analyses using electronic sales data and COVID-19 cases in regions of Italy.  The results show that the proposed test has good performance both in simulations and real-world settings.  The source code for the test and other related methods is available online.  Future work may involve exploring other methods for evaluating network autoregressive models and extending the proposed test to dynamic network autoregressive models.  The theoretical findings are applicable to a broader class of network models, which are discussed in the paper.  Ultimately, we hope that the proposed test will contribute to the development of network time series models that accommodate time-varying coefficients. The mechanical properties of cells are primarily governed by the behavior of stress fibers, which are linked to the cell's motility and tissue interphase force.  To gain a deeper understanding of this mechanism, we developed a unified, active mechanics framework that considers the nonlinear properties of stress fibers and surrounding cytoplasm.  This model effectively predicts both first and third-order stress fiber mechanics when subjected to sudden load applications, as observed in micropipette experiments.  Additionally, it accurately captures the stress fiber's active retraction response when subjected to sustained loads, which is crucial for its long-term mechanical behavior.  By incorporating this stress fiber model into a computational framework, we simulated both cell and tissue mechanics, reproducing observed mechanical phenomena, including power-law relationships between stress and strain in stress fibers and the scaling of cell and tissue forces.  This study provides a comprehensive framework that integrates active and passive cell mechanics, enabling a deeper exploration of cellular mechanobiology.  As an example, we investigated how stress fiber retraction is influenced by molecular motor parameters, load duration, and cell module properties.  Future developments of this framework could be applied to study various cellular mechanisms, such as cell division, differentiation, and motility.  As for stress fiber mechanics, there are opportunities to refine the model by incorporating filament disassembly and reorganization, as observed in live cell imaging.  Ultimately, this study aims to advance stress fiber mechanics through a unified active mechanics framework, offering multiple avenues for further exploration, and its broad applicability to cellular mechanobiology.  As such, it has the potential to become a fundamental tool for computational cell biology. By providing in-guest virtual machine management through dynamic reconfiguration, Argus enhances application performance by minimizing overhead from unnecessary memory reallocation and data copying. Our approach is supported by the findings of a comprehensive memory reconfiguration study, which identified the optimal approach to optimizing memory layout for HPC applications by considering factors like memory allocation strategies, reconfiguration frequencies, and cloud cost structures. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Argus, we conducted several benchmark tests using HPC applications and observed significant performance improvements, with gains ranging from 15% to 60%. Additionally, Argus was compared to other cloud HPC solutions, including BigDisk, HPSurf, and ClouDBurst, and showed superiority over them in terms of performance. Furthermore, we explored the potential for Argus to be implemented using low-level hypervisor technologies similar to VMware vSphere, and examined the implications of doing so. Finally, we discussed strategies for making Argus production-ready, including addressing issues of system instability, managing cloud costs, and integrating it with existing HPC workload managers. Lastly, we outlined potential research paths for enhancing Argus through techniques like live kernel updates, hypervisor-assisted checkpointing, and improved memory reconfiguration methods. Ultimately, Argus provides a viable solution for achieving high performance computing in cloud infrastructure and identifies areas for further improvement. While Scrum methodology has proven effective for in-person collaborations, its suitability for successful projects conducted entirely remotely is unclear. To shed light on this, we examined the connection between Scrum adoption and project success from both the team performance and client perspective. Through a survey aimed at project managers working entirely remotely, our findings revealed the presence of Scrum variables such as product owner effectiveness, product backlog quality, and sprint planning quality which, not surprisingly, displayed positive correlations with project success. Notably, we discovered no significant difference in project success when comparing those using Scrum to other Agile methodologies, yet this difference disappeared once we accounted for team performance. Consequently, we suggest that from a practical perspective, successful remote projects rely on strong team performance. Finally, we propose and partially validated research questions regarding the optimal Scrum implementation for remote projects, worthy of exploration in future studies. By contributing to both the Agile and remote work bodies of knowledge, our study provides initial answers to recently emerging challenges. Despite being based on self-reported data, our results reflect a genuine pattern, as verified by multiple reliability checks. As one of the largest surveys focusing on remote Agile projects, with 4132 respondents, our study offers an extensive and reliable set of findings. These results can be utilized by both researchers and practitioners working on Agile and remote work projects. As such, we hope that this study paves the way for further in-depth investigations within this recently evolving field of study. In policy learning, using temporary data to estimate a policy's value function
through sampling has various applications, including batch policy evaluation and
learning from multiple tasks simultaneously. Although it is known that increasing
the testing sample size improves the accuracy of these estimates, doing so may
exceed available budget when making decisions in real-time. This study investigates
a long-standing conjecture that certain efficient value function estimators, such
as the one proposed by Jia and Song (2020), achieve the optimal trade-off between
test sample size and mean squared error (MSE) regardless of the underlying
transition dynamics. To address this question, we develop a general framework
evaluating the efficacy of these estimators, and counter-theoretic results reveal
that they indeed achieve the optimal test sample size MSE under certain conditions.
Additionally, our framework enables us to investigate how different transition
dynamics affect the performance of these estimators, and counter-examples demonstrate
that some of them may not achieve optimal test sample size MSE in other scenarios.
Finally, our methodological framework is validated through concrete examples and
empirical studies, and a method for selecting the best estimator based on test
sample size is proposed and shown to work well in practice. Notably, our work
also identifies two previously unknown efficient value function estimators, and
finds that one of these newly identified estimators outperforms existing methods
even when the test sample size is very large. As the proposed methods are
applicable to any policy, we also discuss their connections to batch policy
evaluation and multi-task policy learning. Our implementation is available online

We introduce an innovative, high-efficiency computational approach for simulating flows carrying particles of varying sizes in motion. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm, an enhanced version of the TSAP method, organizes the simulation into distinct time segments: a massively parallel stage for the simulation of the flow by integral equation methods, and a second stage with a direct numerical integration method for the simulation of particle interactions. This two-stage approach allows for significant computational gains, achieving up to 100 times faster computation than traditional methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm with two scenarios: suspended particles within a swirling flow over a solid surface, and a simulation of sediment transport with particles ranging from sub-wavelength to several wavelengths in size. Our algorithm is robust, as validated by comparisons with traditional methods and actual experiments, with notable improvements including decreased CPU time, preserved accuracy of both flow and particle velocities, and conformity with kinetic energy spectra of turbulent flows. This algorithm is particularly suited for simulations of flows carrying multiple particles by showcasing extreme scalability on computational clusters, and is an innovative solution to the longstanding problem of efficiently computing particle-laden flows. This research involves developing a robotic hopping mechanism with an elastic foot that allows for precise trajectory tracking on soft surfaces. Unlike stiff-legged robots, an elastic foot experiences delayed and diminished reactions from the ground, affecting the robot's ability to track a straight line. High-frequency oscillations also occur between the foot and the ground, complicating control strategies. To overcome these challenges, a feedback control system was created using a simplified but realistic ground model. The feedback control system was designed to minimize the impact of surface friction and the elastic foot's vibrations on the robot's motion. As a result, the robot was able to track a straight path successfully, even with an overly stiff and oscillatory elastic foot, indicating that the feedback control system is robust to variations in the foot's elasticity. To extend the approach to more complex trajectories, a state-dependent switching control system was developed. This system alternates between the feedback control and an open-loop control, depending on the robot's velocity and acceleration. By doing so, the robot is able to track a curved path with an elastic foot, despite the surface's friction and vibrations, leading to further improvements in its ability to navigate soft environments. To validate the approach, simulations and actual tests on a robotic hopping mechanism were conducted. The results showed that the feedback control system and state-dependent switching control system can be applied to actual robotic hopping mechanisms, leading to more precise trajectory tracking on soft surfaces. This research provides a theoretical and practical framework for developing robust control strategies for robotic hopping mechanisms in various environments and situations. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a novel Bayesian model based on the Bag-of-Words representation that structures documents and terms into two hierarchical layers. Unlike conventional topic modeling approaches, our model segregates documents into exclusive groups, assigns each group a distinct topic distribution, and infers term distributions within each group. We develop an efficient Metropolis-Hasting sampler for parameter estimation and evaluate HDTM on two real-world datasets, comparing it to the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model. Our results indicate that HDTM surpasses LDA in terms of model fit and predictive performance. Furthermore, we examine HDTM's ability to capture semantic relationships among terms and document semantics through a systematic exploration of model parameters. Additionally, we analyze the coherence of topics over time within a historical corpus, providing a method for interpreting time-dependent topics. Through the exploration of two real-world applications, our study demonstrates the efficacy of HDTM in modeling and exploiting network structure and we make publicly available the implementation of our model on the NIPS 2008 dataset, along with a visualization tool that is accessible online. Lastly, we discuss future research directions for hierarchical document models and associated inference techniques. This work is part of the author's Ph.D. thesis.

Quantum annealing is a technique used to find the minimum or maximum of a given function by slowly transforming a system from a state where a target function's optimal value is clearly defined to one where it is obscured. However, the effectiveness of this method relies heavily on the "annealing gap," which is the difference between the target function at its optimal and suboptimal points when the system is critically disturbed. Determining the annealing gap requires solving a complex inverse problem that involves reversing the application of quantum annealing. In this study, we examine the relationship between the annealing gap and two important parameters: the duration of quantum annealing and the strength of its perturbations. We also investigate whether this gap can be optimized through a protocol that manipulates these parameters, which we found to be possible in certain cases by applying a simulated quantum annealing protocol to a specific problem. Additionally, we propose a new quantum annealing schedule that can be considered a hybrid of parallel and sequential applications, which can be effective even when the target function's optimal value is unclear. We further investigate the fundamental limitations of this gap's optimization by examining the maximum probability of finding the target function's optimal value when applying quantum annealing for an infinite duration. This probability was found to be bounded by the annealing gap raised to a power that depends on the strength of the perturbations. Therefore, optimizing the annealing gap is crucial for improving the probability of finding the target function's optimal value. Finally, we examine the relationship between the annealing gap and two types of quantum states: ground states and saddle points, which represent local minima and maxima. We found that the annealing gap can be expressed in terms of the difference between the energies of these states when the system is critically disturbed, which can be used to develop more effective quantum annealing protocols. This understanding of the annealing gap's properties is seen as a crucial step towards improving the probability of finding the target function's optimal value when applying quantum annealing. This will have significant implications for the development of new quantum annealing schedules and the creation of practical applications that can leverage quantum computing's potential. This study's findings are realized through a simulated quantum annealing protocol on a model system consisting of interchangeable spin models, which allows for the precise manipulation of the annealing gap. This protocol and model system are highly versatile and can be easily adapted for use in other applications and environments. This research introduces a novel approach to tracking the evolution of software systems by combining static and dynamic analysis methods. By applying singular value decomposition, we can identify key components called 'features' that remain stable across different versions of the software, even as other components change. Additionally, we determine the scores of each software version's similarity to each feature, which provides valuable insights for maintaining and improving the software. Our method is demonstrated using a case study of the Apache HTTP Server and show how it can help in detecting areas of the software that are sensitive to changes, thus potentially leading to performance degradation. Furthermore, we use these scores to distinguish features that influence convergence time during startup. Our approach also enables the visualization of software components in high-dimensional space, which can aid in pinpointing complex system dynamics and informing maintenance decisions. Finally, we outline possible directions for advancing this research, including the integration of our method with other methods for analyzing software systems and the use of machine learning algorithms to improve feature stability and convergence performance. This study focuses on examining the spread of information and public opinion on
Twitter during the COVID-19 pandemic in India. By analyzing around 500,000 daily
Twitter posts from 25 major Indian cities, our research aims to characterize the
temporal evolution of information and public sentiment in these cities. We used
these findings to evaluate the effectiveness of government responses in controlling
COVID-19 and suppressing misinformation, and also identified factors influencing
these outcomes. We observed temporal variations in data collection and found
temporal differences in data exchange on Twitter with two peaks: one representing
opinion sharing and the other representing fact-sharing. Our results showed that
sentiment in certain cities followed the national pattern, while in others it
deviated from it. Furthermore, our analysis indicated that the relationship between
sentiment and infection rates is non-linear, and that the relationship between
sentiment and infection mortality rates exhibits a linear pattern. We also found
that infection rates and mortality rates are highly correlated. We analyzed the
effect of misinformation on sentiment and found a linear relationship between the
two. We observed that government interventions were often lagged behind in their
effectiveness, and that there is a non-linear relationship between the amount of
data available and the effectiveness of government measures in a city. We found
that high population density and late government intervention can exacerbate the
spread of misinformation. We also found that economic factors have a non-linear
effect on the spread of misinformation, and that there is a linear relationship
between the amount of data available and the effectiveness of government measures
in suppressing misinformation. We believe that our research has implications for
combating the spread of misinformation and reducing public health risks during
pandemics. We hope that our results will be useful to policymakers, public health
officials, and technology companies working to address these challenges. We also
hope that our research will inspire further study of the complex relationships
between data exchange, public opinion, sentiment, and health outcomes during

The success of deep learning-based question answering systems relies on vast amounts of data and computing power, however, incorporating knowledge from large knowledge bases into these systems is complicated. A semantic-driven approach is proposed to simplify this process by utilizing a knowledge graph to identify relevant knowledge for each question, and is demonstrated in a two-step method. First, a knowledge graph is constructed from a knowledge base with the assistance of natural language processing techniques, then at inference time, a graph neural network is applied to this graph to determine the appropriate knowledge for each question. Our method is evaluated on a question answering dataset containing 14,000 questions and incorporating 100,000 knowledge base triples, showing better performance than a random baseline and the current state-of-the-art approach. Additionally, an analysis of the method's reliability and the influence of different graph construction methods on performance is examined. The code for this research is available under an open-source license on GitHub.

well as a new quantity, the effective lag $\rho_{\rm eff}$, which is

challenging due to a lack of clear, standardized evaluation methods and
benchmark data. Existing assessment approaches often rely on simplified
metrics, such as accuracy or ROC-AUC, which do not adequately capture the

testing these models. To address this limitation, we have developed a more
robust assessment framework that considers multiple aspects of model
performance and incorporated it into a comprehensive benchmark dataset called
BASS-Endpoints. This dataset consists of 512 prediction points derived from
well-known pharmacological datasets and serves as a standard for evaluating
and comparing the performance of molecular activity prediction models, graph
classification models, and link prediction models in the field of pharmacology.

accessible benchmark platform that allows researchers to design, execute, and
compare their experiments. By utilizing this framework and benchmark dataset,

area of pharmacology and are making both the benchmark dataset and the
benchmark platform freely available to the entire research community.

The work presents enhanced versions of two significant mathematical concepts: the Young integral and the rough path theory. Introduced initially by Louis-Massiat and Tournus in 2019, and further developed by the same authors in 2020, these results demonstrate the capacity to handle functions with multiple increments beyond the BMP (Bourdon, Cass, and Lyons) continuity standard, specifically able to handle functions with more than two continuous increments in this paper. Additionally, this research demonstrates that approximating a function with multiple increments is equivalent to approximating the corresponding rough path, which is a fundamental component in the study of differential equations. This finding is key to extending the theory of rough paths to a broader class of functions. Furthermore, this development is coupled with a new criterion for when a function with multiple increments has a continuous extension, which is essential for the theory of rough paths. This new criterion is a significant improvement, as it is more flexible than previous standards, and it enables researchers to explore a broader class of stochastic differential equations. This research is also accompanied by an example demonstrating that approximating a function with more than two continuous increments may not always be equivalent to approximating the corresponding rough path. This example raises further questions and motivates ongoing research in this field. This work is a crucial precursor to addressing related problems, such as the existence and uniqueness of the rough integral and the solution to stochastic differential equations. It is anticipated that this new standard will contribute to improved results related to the Young integral, which is a foundational component of rough path theory, and may potentially lead to improved results for related concepts, such as the Divergence integral. This development is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of rough paths and facilitate further research in this field. This work is an essential milestone in the ongoing quest to expand the capacity of rough path theory. We present an analytical model to study the dynamics of inertial wave turbulence on a
finite, rotating sphere. We break down the self-sustaining patterns into two categories,
based on the number of hemispheres they occupy, and derive the energy spectrum for each
category. Our results show that the spectrum follows $k^x \cdot k_y^x$ for waves with distinct
non-zero frequencies, a law previously observed on infinite domains. We find that this
law applies to all but the most highly resonant modes. For resonant modes, the spectrum
becomes self-similar, with the same form as found for shallow water turbulence on an
infinite plane. We validate our model using data from a rotating sphere filled with
viscous fluid, and compare it to a self-similar model derived by wave action density.
Our analysis reveals that the self-similar model overestimates the amplitude of the
coherent structures by a factor of $\sim 3$ when applied to finite domains. We also
find that the coherent structures with higher energies are able to maintain themselves
through a continuous process of breaking down into smaller scales, while those with
lower energies are eventually dissipated. Our research provides a theoretical framework
for analyzing inertial wave turbulence on finite domains, and sheds light on the
mechanisms that govern the persistence of coherent structures in turbulent flows.

A alternative method involves utilizing feature importance from an exact model, but this can be challenging when dealing with multiple mental health conditions.  Another approach involves using mutual information to determine the connection between each mental health condition and the likelihood of recidivism, but this method may produce inconsistent results due to the diversity of data sets.  To address these limitations, three distinct methods were evaluated to determine the most reliable way to identify the mental health conditions most closely linked to a higher likelihood of recidivism.  The results show that the conditions associated with a greater likelihood of recidivism are personality disorders, anxiety disorders, and mood disorders.  The findings also highlight the challenges in assessing the relationship between each mental health condition and the likelihood of recidivism due to the limited information available for some conditions.  To address this issue, collecting more comprehensive data on mental health conditions in conjunction with justice system data is necessary. Rendering 3D dynamic objects from a single 2D image is a key goal of
computer vision. Recent advances in neural rendering have demonstrated
significant progress in this area, but they are primarily geared towards
static scenes. To expand this work to render moving objects, a major
shortfall in existing frameworks is the absence of articulation. For example,
they fail to account for the fact that a person's eyes move in tandem with
their head. To address this limitation, we introduce Articulated Neural
Rendering, a framework that not only allows for rendering dynamic objects
using neural textures, but also considers articulation. We validated our
approach using a large dataset of faces and heads derived from the
Multi-PIE database and found that our method not only surpasses previous face
rendering techniques but also yields accurate results for head rendering.
Further, we demonstrate that our approach can be applied to render other
articulated objects, such as bodies, by integrating available scanning
techniques and neutral avatars. To facilitate future research, we will
make our framework and data available for public access. All code and
datasets can be found at https://github.com/ivanhofer/Articulated_NR. A
supplementary video for this work may be viewed at
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Q6c8Qy1QgA.

We examine the performance of speech recognition systems when applying transfer learning across languages with varying levels of similarity. Our assessment indicates that speech recognition systems are capable of learning universal representations that facilitate successful application in languages different from the training data. This capability allows us to achieve a significant reduction in the necessary training data for languages with limited data, including low-resource languages and languages distinct from the training set. Our findings reveal that multilingual models excel in languages with some similarity, such as Italian and Spanish, and languages sharing the same script, such as Hindi and Marathi, with a notable 5.3% improvement in accuracy. Moreover, we observe that speech recognition systems can successfully apply knowledge from one language to another, even across substantial gaps, as evident in our experiments with languages as dissimilar as English and Telugu, with a notable 11.3% improvement in low-data conditions. Our exploration of various transfer learning strategies and data augmentation techniques guides the design of more effective speech recognition systems for low-resource languages and languages distinct from the training set. We also introduce the Zero-Resource Speech Recognition dataset, which includes 10 languages for training and 5 for testing, with a total of around 2000 hours of data. Our results on this dataset demonstrate that transfer learning achieves accurate performance on languages without any specific data or labels, with an overall improvement of 8.8% in accuracy compared to the baseline model. Notably, our approach enables successful application of knowledge from one language to another, even across substantial gaps, with a notable 11.3% improvement in low-data conditions. We anticipate that our analysis and findings will contribute to breakthroughs in speech recognition systems for low-resource languages and languages distinct from the training set.
