However, if the increments are independent and identically distributed with an average of zero and no other specific characteristics, then the asymptotic distribution of the walk may vary based on a parameter that determines the rate at which the walk's components change. This rate is represented by a parameter 'b' that is unique to each set of independently distributed increments. If 'b' is greater than zero, then the asymptotic distribution of the walk relies on 'b'. Otherwise, the asymptotic distribution is independent of 'b'. Optimizing plasma sources is crucial for plasma applications and could be achieved by understanding the underlying physics of plasma production. For low-temperature plasmas, electron temperature and density play significant roles in source performance. This study investigates the effects of electron temperature and density on plasma sources, considering both laminar and turbulent plasma flows. A quasineutral plasma model was used to analyze the impact of electron temperature and density on plasma resistance, Reynolds number, and the transition between laminar and turbulent flows. Numerical simulations showed that sources with high electron temperatures and densities tend to have lower plasma resistance and favor turbulent flows. However, above a certain limit, further increase in these parameters does not significantly affect plasma resistance. A dimensionless source performance index was then proposed to correlate with plasma sources' resistance, Reynolds number, and the laminar-turbulent transition. This index was applied to analyze various plasma sources, revealing distinct performance patterns for interdigital, coplanar, and disk-shaped sources. Interestingly, sources with high electron temperatures and densities tend to follow the same performance curve, indicating that source performance is primarily governed by electron density. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for developing a comprehensive source performance prediction model and could guide the empirical design of plasma sources. Furthermore, this study introduces a new framework for source performance classification, suggesting that the choice of source should be steered by specific plasma requirements in treatment applications. Ultimately, optimizing plasma sources is seen as an essential step in achieving the maximum symbiotic effect between plasma and semiconductors. This work is believed to lay the groundwork for a more in-depth investigation into source performance and could have broader implications for the understanding of plasma sources in various contexts. Lastly, future research directions are outlined, including the extension of source performance classification to account for additional factors and the exploration of a source performance index for high-temperature plasmas. Nucleus detection is a fundamental skill in medical research and research aided by computer vision. The accuracy of subsequent analysis, such as nucleus phase and cell cycle stage, depends heavily on the accuracy of the detected nucleus. Existing nucleus detection methods primarily employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with two branches: one for target finding and one for background removal. These methods end with a simple binarization step that converts the output to a nucleus mask. Here we propose the W-shaped network, an advanced detector that incorporates two advanced techniques: nested nested Mask R-CNNs for target detection and nested FPNs for background removal. By combining these two sets of expert features the W-shaped network has shown significant improvements over the baseline method in various benchmark datasets. Not only does it achieve higher precision and recall rates but it has also demonstrated the ability to operate with much less training data. When trained on the CPM dataset with 6000 images the W-shaped network achieved a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.9382, outperforming the baseline method by 0.0175. When trained on the Spacenet dataset with 15000 images the W-shaped network achieved a mAP of 0.9733, surpassing the baseline by 0.0081 in terms of precision and 0.0053 in terms of recall. What's more the W-shaped network has been found to have a much higher efficiency compared to traditional methods, with an FPS rate of 20.35, an improvement of 11.6 over the baseline method. Further, this new method will be used to improve upon existing formulas for calculating the Hamiltonian path index of certain cyclic graphs. Specifically, the paper will derive a more efficient formula for calculating the Hamiltonian path index of a cyclic graph composed of distinct vertex degrees, effectively providing a new approach that surpasses the current recursive method. This innovative approach will be demonstrated through a sample calculation of a cyclic graph with known degree measures. Lastly, the paper will introduce a new concept, referred to as "Hamiltonian path cover" and will explore its connection to the Hamiltonian path index. Finally, several open questions will be posed to stimulate further research.

This issue arises when trying to combine the symmetries using both the given boundary CFT and the non-invertible symmetry itself. To tackle this problem, we use the TFA for both $ext{QCD}$ in a rectangular box and the $SU(3)$ SYM theory in a rectangular box to compute the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries in $ext{QCD}$. We find that these rules are related to the structure of the Weyl group in $SU(3)$. Furthermore, we derive the central charge of the stress tensor for the symmetric product states, which involves a sum over the momenta of the Weyl group orbits. This calculation is verified by analyzing the one-loop partition function in $SU(3)$ SYM theory using the HFTHA. We also explore the application of these results to the study of non-invertible symmetries in $SU(3)$ SYM theory. To extend these results to other gauge groups, we propose a related Weyl group for each simple gauge algebra and examine its properties. This framework is then utilized to examine the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries in $SU(3)$ SYM theory, and a notable consequence of this structure is the appearance of orbifolds in the spectrum. To validate this, we compare our computations to direct orbifold calculations for a pair of non-invertible symmetries corresponding to a charge $<2$ angle in $SU(3)$ SYM theory. Lastly, we discuss how these results for the fusion rules may be used in conjunction with the HAHA to reconstruct the gauge interactions in the HAHA for $SU(3)$ SYM theory. We develop a one-pass algorithm for creating a coreset for the $k$-means clustering problem. Our method involves selecting a representative subset of $k$ points from a given dataset of $n$ points, and this selection can be accomplished in a single pass through the dataset. We ensure that the coreset's size is proportional to $k$ times the minimum number of points required to solve the $k$-means problem with an error of $\epsilon$. Specifically, our coreset's size is $O(k \cdot f(\epsilon, k, n, \{x_i\}))$, where $f(\epsilon, k, n, \{x_i\})$ is the number of points required to achieve $\epsilon$-approximation for the $k$-means problem. We construct the coreset by selecting points that are closest to the median of their respective clusters, and we demonstrate that this approach results in a coreset with the desired properties. Notably, our one-pass algorithm outperforms multi-pass algorithms in terms of efficiency, and we validate its performance through experimental evaluations. In large domain grid worlds, complex scenarios can be broken down into simpler components called superstates, whose individual analysis simplifies decision-making. This concept is particularly useful in pursuit-evasion scenarios. By identifying superstates and their corresponding policies, a controller can effectively manage multiple encounters within the domain. However, determining optimal actions in each superstate requires significant computational resources. An alternative approach involves using a learning algorithm like DQN on a simplified grid representation, but its efficacy is limited by the depth of its tree search. An emerging alternative involves policy-based methods like virtual state modeling, which learns action values for each grid state individually. These models struggle to scale to larger domains due to their high computational cost and memory requirements. This research introduces an iterative Monte Carlo tree search algorithm that efficiently handles complex pursuit-evasion scenarios in large grid domains by learning action values for each superstate. The algorithm's performance is on par with existing state-of-the-art methods, such as VSM, in terms of efficiency, but its computational cost is significantly lower. This is achieved by training each superstate model in isolation, after which the entire domain is re-scanned to identify new superstates. The research demonstrates that high-performance, grid-based solutions for pursuit-evasion scenarios can be implemented efficiently using Monte Carlo tree search methods, and that these methods are particularly effective at scaling to larger domains. An open-source implementation of the algorithm is also provided, along with suggestions for further improving its efficiency. This research offers an innovative approach to handling complex scenarios in grid-based pursuit-evasion games and may have broader implications for the application of iterative learning algorithms in complex domains. This research is relevant to any field that uses grid-based worlds, and it is therefore accessible to a broad range of researchers and practitioners in the artificial intelligence community. This is further highlighted by the author's own experience with grid-based games during the 2019 General Game Learning Competition. This research is published as part of the Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) workshop on anyworld games, and it is the author's hope that it will contribute to the ongoing development of iterative learning algorithms and the study of complex scenarios in grid-based games. A nonstandard definition of a nontransitive n-tuple has been proposed, where an n-tuple of distinct positive integers is considered nontransitive if it cannot be represented in the form of an ordered triple using the same integer values, whose corresponding entries in reverse order still allow it to satisfy the original condition. We aim to expand on a particular case of this definition, specifically for 3-tuples, where the condition is met if the sum of the two middle numbers is greater than the two outer numbers, and this condition is true for all permutations of the 3-tuple. Our goal is to examine 3-tuples that meet this nontransitive criterion and provide a relationship between their elements, along with a maximum value, which we then use to identify all possible nonstandard 4-tuples that meet the same condition. Furthermore, we derive a method to generate any desired nonstandard 3-tuple or 4-tuple that meets the condition, and we also establish a limit on the maximum possible value of the greatest element in a nonstandard 3-tuple or 4-tuple. Lastly, we establish a connection between the nontransitive 3-tuples and a well-known Diophantine equation, and we present a new way to express a particular class of solutions to this equation using a nonstandard 3-tuple that satisfies the given condition. 

Keywords: Nontransitive n-tuple, positive integers, number theory, Diophantine equation.

This study proposes an innovative use of adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers to combine interpretable components for a cycleGAN in the creation of a cycleGAN based on image transformations, specifically using UNets and Fourier-based discriminators. Our model segregates and reorders the data and style codes within reverse mapping functions, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art methods using only two codes, without employing adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers or circle GANs. We further demonstrate that incorporating AdaIN layers as simple AdaIN layers, instead of circle GANs, significantly enhances the performance of our basic cycleGAN design. Our findings indicate that AdaIN layers play a significant role in unlearning unnecessary information during the mapping process. We also provide concrete mathematical evidence for this phenomenon by analyzing the adjoints of the forward and reverse mappings. We have made our code publicly available on the MIST platform.

This paper provides a detailed explanation of the interface variable PDFs for W and Z bosons, extending the work of Buckley et al. by incorporating universal corrections to the boson PDFs. We calculate the boson PDFs at NNLL accuracy and the corresponding anomalous dimensions at NNLO, using a Collins-Sotiropoulos representation to connect the boson PDFs to the corresponding dijet functions. We also derive the evolution equation for the boson PDFs, solving it to obtain the universal Collins-Sotiropoulos representation of the boson PDFs in terms of the corresponding split-hadron distributions. This enables us to determine the x-dependence of the boson PDFs at a given scale, even if the initial conditions are unknown. As an example, we consider the boson PDFs relevant to Higgs boson production in association with a vector boson. We find that the universal corrections shift the corresponding combination of quark PDFs by approximately 10% at NNLL accuracy, with an x-dependent shift that is significant at NNLL compared to NNL. This implies that experimental determinations of quark PDFs from Higgs boson data will also be shifted by a comparable amount, depending on how they are extracted. We also find that the corresponding combination of gluon PDFs is less affected, with a shift of approximately 1% at NNLL accuracy. This is because the dominant contribution to the boson PDF comes from the twist-2 component, which is primarily driven by the quark distribution. As a result, the change to the boson PDF is largely captured by the change to the quark PDF. This shift is not an artifact of the particular choice of process, as it is also seen in the case of dijet production, which is a more fundamental process influenced by the same quark PDF. Therefore, experimental determinations of quark PDFs from dijet data will also be shifted by a comparable amount, depending on how they are extracted. In contrast, the gluon PDF is shifted by less than 1% at NNLL accuracy in this case as well. We argue that these shifts reflect universal corrections to the quark PDFs, as they are primarily driven by the quark distribution and not process-dependent. They therefore have implications for the extraction of quark PDFs from a variety of experimental data. In this work, we investigate whether multiple dynamics models can be an effective solution for multi-task reinforcement learning problems. We contribute two key findings to this research: First, simply combining multiple models does not yield meaningful improvements. Secondly, we discovered that simply using an exploration strategy that takes into account the individual strengths and weaknesses of each model produces substantially better results. To further build on these insights, we developed an algorithm that adapts the exploration strategy on a per-task basis in real-time by optimizing a virtual reward that considers the performance and confidence of each model. This is achieved without requiring prior knowledge of task dynamics or difficulties. We evaluated our approach using both theoretical and practical methods, with results showing superior performance compared to baseline methods on complex multi-task scenarios. End-to-end direct regression has emerged as a prominent approach for camera calibration, particularly for the focal length and lens radius of spherical surfaces. We challenge this specialized focus by developing a comprehensive direct regression model that simultaneously determines multiple camera parameters, including the focal length, lens radius, distortion coefficients, and rotation and translation vectors. While classical methods first estimate individual components before combining them, our unified model learned from synthetic data surpasses the accuracy of traditional methods on real-world datasets. We also examine the challenges of applying these models in real-world scenarios and find that simply using clean data is not enough to replicate the performance seen in synthetic domains. We discovered that directly regressing on noisy real data yields inferior results to classical methods. To overcome this limitation, we fine-tuned our pre-trained model on real data with data augmentation, ultimately achieving comparable performance to classical methods and even outperforming them in certain scenarios. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring direct regression on other camera calibration tasks and considers the challenges of applying learned models to real-world scenarios. We also established a public repository for our code and dataset, taking the initial step towards advancing the field. Additionally, our research highlights the potential of combining classical and deep learning approaches to camera calibration. We identified potential avenues for improvement, including the use of self-supervision and additional training data, and believe these topics are worthy of further investigation. We hope our study will motivate others to explore direct regression and related topics within camera calibration. We have made our code and dataset publicly available. 

Keywords: camera calibration, direct regression, deep learning, classical methods, dataset availability, code availability.

However, implementing beam training in such scenarios is often impractically slow and expensive for terahertz systems due to their high transmission costs. To address this issue, a new method is proposed for efficient dynamic beam training in multi-hop wireless networks. In this approach, a joint learning algorithm is trained at the transmitter using data from the receiver, and training is adapted in real-time based on data delivery performance. A new recurrent neural network model called the BRNN is introduced, which uses a cascaded layout with two hidden layers to significantly reduce computational requirements while achieving improved performance in modeling speech and other quasi-periodic signals. The proposed model is then used to analyze the fundamental limitations of hidden Markov models (HMMs) and the challenges they pose for sequential neural network models. It is shown that HMMs, despite being fundamental to sequence modeling, can suffer from over-simplification and over-fitting, which can be mitigated in the BRNN by re-purposing the cascaded layout as a multi-periodicity detector. This approach allows the network to focus on accurate modeling of individual sub-units within quasi-periodic signals, thereby overcoming the fundamental limitations of HMMs. The BRNN is demonstrated to outperform not just HMMs but also other sequential neural network models, including simple RNNs and LSTM/HMM hybrids, in terms of both inference and training efficiency. The advantages of the BRNN are further validated through both speech synthesis and recognition tasks. The source code for the proposed model is available online.

We introduce the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), an innovative graph convolutional network (GCN) for operating within the realm of hyperbolic space. Current hyperbolic GCNs utilize a parametric transformation at each graph convolution layer to adjust the underlying hypersphere, however these transformations are not explicitly learned during training. In contrast, the Lorentzian graph CNN utilizes the intrinsic geometry of hyperbolic space, specifically the exponential map and Jacobian matrix, to perform a non-parametric transformation of node features. We demonstrate that this approach not only learns more accurate and robust representations of node features for both the training and testing datasets but also outperforms existing hyperbolic GCNs on multiple benchmark datasets. The code for the Lorentzian graph CNN is openly available at https://github.com/zhengdf1123/LGCN.

We've proposed a scheme using a photonic crystal cavity with a hybrid optomechanical setup to physically demonstrate Thouless symmetry breaking through a boundary state effect. This setup involves an optical mode and a mechanical mode with identical parity properties, shared across two spatial regions divided by an opaque mirror. One region's optical mode has high amplitude near the boundary, corresponding to the 1st optical band. We calculate the optomechanical response, specifically the first-order optical shift, to assess the symmetry effect. We also investigate various parameters, including optomechanical coupling strength, laser power, and the mechanical loss, finding that they all follow the same symmetry pattern. To visualize the TSS, we use a scanning optical near-field technique to show the interband optomechanical response when the mechanical mode is tuned to an anti-crossing with a nearby optical mode, revealing an asymmetrical pattern on either side of the boundary. We suggest that this TSS effect could be used as a standard for testing the surface state of TIs. Additionally, we propose modifying the setup to detect TSS in MEs by incorporating a spin-pump mechanism to inject spin polarization into the surface state. We examine the spin-pump mechanism and find that it allows for the detection of TSS in MEs, providing an alternative method for identifying MEs with TSS. This detection method could potentially be applied to other systems involving interband optomechanical interactions between surface states and bulk modes. We anticipate that this could lead to the development of new techniques for analyzing the electronic properties of MEs in optomechanical systems. We explore an extension of the $u$-calculus, specifically within a polymorphic framework, by incorporating atomic operations that modify argument variables. This expansion results in a heightened expression power and a complexity shift in determining satisfiability in atomic $u$-calculus formulas; in fact, atomic $u$-calculus becomes undecidable. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that determining satisfiability in atomic $u$-calculus is decidable when restricted to formulas without infinite ascending chains. Moreover, we analyze the atomic $u$-calculus within the context of multiplicative and additive linear logic. Systematically, we examine the relationship between atomic $u$-calculus and the provability of formulas in linear logic. Ultimately, we establish that atomic $u$-calculus can simulate cut-elimination in linear logic, hinting that atomic $u$-calculus may provide a computational interpretation of linear logic's structural rules. This study offers a foundational framework for exploring the interplay between combinators, atomic operations, and $u$-calculus within a polymorphic context. Hybrid quantum classical (HQC) methods integrate classical Hamiltonian dynamics with quantum mechanics, offering a potential bridge between thermodynamic and quantum theories. However, their validity depends on the type of quantum state and Hamiltonian used. Recently, research has identified quantum equilibrium states that maintain equilibrium under classical and quantum dynamics, providing a strong basis for HQC simulations. This study expands on that research by examining four fundamental classical dynamics scenarios: reversible, dissipative, stochastic, and mixed processes. It is shown that only reversible processes can be accurately replicated using classical dynamics in HQC simulations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that using the time-average classical trajectory can accurately simulate reversible processes. It is also found that this approach can also be applied to equilibrium states expressed as mixtures of classical and quantum components. Ultimately, this study suggests that time-average classical trajectories provide a suitable mean-field approximation for simulating HQC simulations for reversible processes. This finding can be particularly useful for simulating chemical reactions using HQC methods. We introduce Generalized Spherical Multipoles (GSMs), a general framework for
describing the interaction between fields and systems, based on an efficient
expansion using generalized spherical multipoles. This approach is highly
effective for the scattering of electromagnetic radiation and other long-range
interactions, and is otherwise versatile for modeling local interactions. A
set of rules allows for the systematic generation of coupled equations for the
multipole moments, and we demonstrate GSM's utility with three example
systems: charge particles in motion; photonic multipoles consisting of dipoles
of different sizes and optical properties; and traditional multipoles
consisting of charges with specific optical properties corresponding to
different multipoles. Additionally, we explore GSM's capabilities in
accommodating external fields and absorbing surfaces, and discuss its
applicability to a variety of scenarios, including systems with multiple units
and components with internal long-range interactions. A simple example
demonstrates how GSM can be employed to derive coupled equations, and a discussion
on different approximation methods for the multipoles' equations is also
included. A Python package known as PyGSM is also available for utilizing
GSM's functionality. This approach has the potential to streamline the
derivation and analysis of coupled equations for complex systems experiencing
long-range interactions, and can serve as a unifying framework for various
multipole theories. A brief description of the PyGSM package is provided for
each of the three example systems mentioned earlier in the text. The PyGSM
package can be particularly useful for simplifying the process of deriving
coupled equations and for analyzing the behavior of complex systems experiencing
long-range interactions, and is available online at https://github.com/akr3094/PyGSM. All PyGSM features are also illustrated with a numerical example involving a rotating dipole system.
